subtopic: MOBILIZATION ACT AMENDMENT BILL-PROGRESS OP SESSIONAL BUSINESS
speechtext:
In reply to my hon. friend I would say that that depends upon the progress which the house makes with the legislation which is before it at the present time. I need not tell my hon. friend that the government is anxious to get on with the business of the session, and the bill to which he has referred is one of the most important of the session. It is our wish to proceed with it at an early day. But it will not be proceeded with until the present war appropriation bill has been completed. The house has already given some four or five weeks to that particular bill, and I should hope that it would be possible to conclude its consideration, along with one or two other small measures, this week. I should hope it would be possible to go on with the other bill some day next week.
I would direct the attention of hon. members to the fact that up to the present time there has been practically no supply considered by the house, and the budget has still to be brought down. There are one or two other important measures on the order paper, and of necessity there may be further legislation before the present session is over- not that I am aware of any at present, but usually something unforeseen crops up at the last moment. If we are to get through before autumn I think we should begin very soon to make more rapid headway than has been made up to the present time. I am not at all sure that it might not be advisable in connection with further proceedings of the house to divide the days between some of the different measures, rather than to sit continuously in discussion of one particular measure. Might I in that connection say further that in my opinion some of the matters being dealt with under the war appropriation bill would be more properly dealt with in supply of the departments concerned. I do not refer to the defence departments. I am told it is the desire to consider some matters with relation to the Department of Agriculture, and if that were to take the form
of a discussion in committee of supply we might have the whole discussion over again when we are in committee of supply. Perhaps time might be saved if the matters to which references are made in the discussion on the war appropriation bill were confined to that bill itself.

To a large extent I agree with what the Prime Minister has said; but may I point out to him that while we are in the seventy-second sitting day of the session, we took twenty-one sitting days in the debate on the address. In those twenty-one days we heard no less than ninety supporters of the government. Then we were asked to put through to a conclusion another measure brought forth by the government, namely the plebiscite bill. Over half of the time of the house has been occupied in the discussion of those two matters.
With respect to the war appropriation bill I would point out that this is the largest money bill which has come before parliament, and I do not think our time has been lost in discussing it. It is the one occasion on which private members have the opportunity, and I say the duty, to investigate what the armed forces and the defence departments are doing. I suggest that the government should have brought on the ordinary estimates before this. There has been opportunity. The whole matter is in the hands of the government. They have taken authority to give government orders precedence; the order of business of the day is as the government directs,. and the responsibility is on the leader of the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Resolved,	that	a	sum	not	exceeding
$38,803,172.40, being one-sixth of the amount of each of the several items to be voted, as set forth in the estimates for the fiscal year ending 31st March, 1943, laid before the House of Commons at the present session of parliament, be granted to His Majesty, on account, for the fiscal year ending 31st March, 1943.
Resolved	that	a	sum	not	exceeding
$1,101,311.83, being one-sixth of the amount of each of the several following items to be voted, as set forth in the estimates for the fiscal year ending 31st March, 1943, laid before the House of Commons at the present session of parliament, in addition to the sum mentioned in resolution No. 1, be granted to His Majesty, on account, for the fiscal year ending 31st March, 1943, namely Nos. 31, 80, 116, 117, 128, 129 and 300.
He said: I am asking for two months' supply, that is one-sixth of the main estimates. It is necessary to have some interim supply voted because only one-sixth was voted before, and that runs out at the end of May. We are now nearly at the end of May, and some provision has to be made for payment of the public service and other obligations of the government in the next month or two. I am requesting therefore that two months' supply be voted, because it is very doubtful whether the estimates will be through before the end of July. Certainly they will not be through before the end of June.

Mr. Chairman, on account of considerations which were adverted to by the Prime Minister and myself a few moments ago, we find ourselves now in the seventy-second sitting day of the session without having voted any supply. The major part of the session up to the time of the introduction and discussion of the war appropriation resolutions was more or less of a political character. Parliament primarily in times of peace is called upon to vote supply, but for seventy-two days this parliament has been in session and no supply has been voted to his majesty. 1 suggest that all through these war sessions the government has not pursued the proper procedure, in putting off the voting of supply until the dying days of the session. In the interim they come to the House of Commons and ask for one-sixth now and one-sixth

Interim. Supply Bill
again. What does that mean? It means that until the end of July they need not ask the house to go into committee of supply. I do not think that that is a proper procedure for the government to pursue.
There are two fundamental objectives of parliament in the ordinary course of proceedings. One is to vote supply to his majesty and the other is to provide ways and means of securing money. Both those considerations have so far been ignored. I do not think the government is justified in asking for a second one-sixth of these appropriations, especially in view of the fact that while we vote the money on the peace-time estimates as well as on the war-time appropriation, parliament is given practically no accounting of how the money is being spent. If you do not believe that, examine the auditor general's report as it stands to-day. In other words, parliament is being asked to vote money en bloc twice in the earlier stages of this session and then to put through the final votes with a rush at the end of the session. That is not treating the members of the House of Commons properly. I protest against this kind of procedure, and I protest against a whole one-sixth being voted to-day.
I realize that the minister has intimated that we are near the end of the fourth month of the session, that the interim supply already granted will run out on the 31st day of May, and that if we do not pass some interim supply to-day, or between now and the 31st, some people, including members of parliament, may have to go without their salaries or indemnities. Well, it would not hurt hon. members if they had to go without the indemnity for a little while, if we could be brought to a realization of the true function and position of parliament. I protest against the granting of one-sixth; I am willing to grant one-twelfth, and that is as far as I am going. I am not going to start a filibuster against this measure, I shall not do anything of the sort. But I ask the minister to confine himself to one-twelfth, especially in view of the fact that he was very generously treated on a former occasion when he asked for one-sixth.
This is the seventy-second sitting day of the session. We spent twenty-one days on the debate on the address. The government could have brought in supply at any time. Then came the plebiscite bill. The Prime Minister says that that would have gone through immediately had I not taken the position I did. I wonder whether it is the thought of the Prime Minister that the opposition in this house should abdicate its functions. We have a responsibility to the
country just as much as the Prime Minister or the government. It is true that it is lesser in degree; nevertheless there is a distinct responsibility on the official opposition; and if we had let the plebiscite bill go through without discussion, unquestionably we would have been recreant to our duty.
After that came the billion dollar resolution and the bill based thereon. That was not held up. We supported that measure and helped to put it through. Then came the resolution on the war appropriation of two billion dollars. I do say at the risk of repeating myself that while that debate is long and is bound to be long, it affords the one occasion in this session when the people of Canada, on the anvil of discussion, can bring out the truth, so far as the government is willing to reveal it, in relation to the war effort of this country. Any time that is spent on the war appropriation bill is time well spent, and I believe I am in the judgment of the country when I make that statement. If the minister gets this one-sixth through tc-day he need not bring up the question of supply until the end of July when the heat of summer will be on us and everyone will be crazy to get home. It is not a right position for the government to take and I protest.

In the main, I support the contention of the leader of the opposition. I believe the time has come when the rules of the house ought to be revised. There was a time when, as the leader of the opposition has said, the main function of this house was the granting of supply and finding ways and means to give that supply to the government. But times have changed and to-day this house has the responsibility of supervising and inquiring into vast economic undertakings and of assuming responsibility in a larger way than ever before for social conditions and social legislation. The result is that parliament's function has to a very large extent been extended in the last twenty years or so, and consequently members come here not only to supervise the expenditure of money and to find ways and means of granting it to the crown, but also to advance social policies now of permanent interest to the community and to inquire into the vast economic undertakings which now belong properly to the government and will probably in future years be extended. I know that at Westminster the rules have been changed to some extent so that the government from time to time sets aside- certain periods when certain things are under discussion and are expected to be discussed within that limited time. They hawe a time table, as my hon. friend the member for Vancouver
Interim Supply Bill

East (Mr. Maclnnis) suggests to me. The same is true, I know, in New Zealand, in Australia and in other parliaments across the world. Our function as a parliament has greatly changed and extended and it seems to me that we are trying to operate under rules which no longer altogether meet the situation under which we are operating.
I agree with the leader of the opposition that it is wrong in principle for this house to grant supply for two months and then two months again, without going into the matter more carefully than we are able to do to-day. That does not imply any lack of confidence in the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) or the officials of his department, or the government generally, but I think it is unsafe and unsound that we grant vast sums of money to the government without adequate and proper inquiry and discussion. I also agree with the leader of the opposition that the war expenditures bill which is now before us, granting to the government the most stupendous sum that we have ever been called upon to vote, ought to be the subject of most careful inquiry in this house, even if it is a prolonged inquiry. I think, however, that if the opposition groups as well as the government would endeavour to departmentalize their own activities a little bit and assign to members of their groups criticism on behalf of the whole group we should probably facilitate the business of the house as opposition groups. We have tried to do that in our little group, and perhaps this has been noticed from time to time. I think that upon the opposition as well as upon the government some responsibility for facilitating the business of the house really rests. In the main, I repeat, I agree with the general criticism of the leader of the opposition.

I cannot agree with the leader of the opposition but to-day I will express similar views. This is the old discussion. I am a supporter of the government and the Minister of Finance is a personal friend of mine, as he knows. If I rise to-day it is because of the promise that was made to me by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) last year, that the public accounts would be prepared more carefully this year than they were last year. Unfortunately, according to what the leader of the opposition said during the course of my remarks on March 17, no item below $35,000 now appears in the public accounts. This is a serious matter. Members should be given an opportunity to secure more detailed information from the auditor general. We have two sources of information with regard to public expenditure. In the first place we 
have the estimates, and secondly we have the public accounts. As to the estimates, I find that there is a great difference between ours and those in the United States. The other day I mentioned the budget which is yearly presented to congress by the President of the United States, and I said that it was a big book the size of the telephone directories of the city of New York, probably two of them, Bronx and Manhattan, bound together. Here I hold in my hand that very official document which was published in Washington, D.C., this year and which is entitled "The budget of the United States government for the fiscal year ending June 30, 1943". It is the budget of the United States at war. I observe with deep regret that British parliamentary traditions are better kept in the United States Congress than they are in the Canadian House of Commons. For instance here at page 764 start the estimates for the navy. They are rather detailed. They extend from page 764 to page 819. I have already said in this house that during the war there should be no secret about money expenditures. I protested with the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) when he complained that the war expenditures committee was sitting behind closed doors. Hitler can get no help from knowing what amount of money is spent in this country for war purposes. It will not improve his chances in any way; therefore I do not understand why such a committee is sitting behind closed doors. And I cannot understand why it is that in the United States they can have such detailed estimates for the navy, and we cannot have them here. However I was pleased to congratulate the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services on the way he handled his war estimates in committee of the whole.
But that is not all. There are also very detailed estimates for the war department in the very same United States budget for the next fiscal year. They extend from page 895 to page 964, with all details. The United States take war seriously, they do it very well, and of course the President of the United States is well enough qualified as a business man and as a shrewd diplomat not to put in his budget anything that would handicap the war effort of his country. Here we have it, and it is a big book.
It is a big countiy.

It is a big book for a big country and for a great war effort.
I heard the Prime Minister say-I do not know whether these are his exact words, but

Interim Supply Bill
they express the meaning of what he said- that some time has been wasted since the beginning of this session. It is my contention that the very reason why the discussion has continued so long with regard to the tremendous amounts spent for war is that we have no detailed estimates about war expenditures in this country. If we had them the discussion would have been much shorter; we would have proceeded in the same way as we did in years past, and after an item had been adopted no hon. member would have been allowed to discuss it again. If there are repetitions in the discussion of that war expenditure it is precisely because hon. members have no guidance in the matter; the discussion jumps from one subject to another in complete disorder and complete chaos.
I was greatly surprised when that course was followed. I regret to have to say that I foresaw that, and I warned the government about the danger of adopting this new practice. No member of the government can complain about any private member discussing fully before this committee any matter regarding expenditure. That right will not be denied. Since it is an unquestionable right, hon. members cannot be blamed for taking advantage of it and using it.
May I ask the government, in the first place, if the statement made by the leader of the opposition is correct that amounts below $35,000 do not now appear in the public accounts? If that is so, why has that course been followed? Secondly, why did the government not put in the estimates detailed information about the expenditures of the war departments? These questions seem reasonable. I should like also to know if it is because it would impede or decrease or handicap our war effort, and if so, how is it that the United States give precisely the information that we have been asking for? As everybody knows, they are doing very well in their war effort. I am ready to give the government a chance on this motion, but this is the last time.
There is another thing I want to tell the house. For many years past I have complained of the intelligentsia. I find that the men who are the arbiters or the high pundits of finance and who are graduates in economics, social science and so on are a curse to all the countries of the world. I say that as a war measure the teaching of economics and social science in universities should be stopped at once, and that all those who are doctors in economics or doctors in political and social science should be fired at once from government jobs. We see now the prodromes of a revolution that existed in Russia before the
communists took power in that country at the end of the last war. I love my country, and I want to see sound reasoning in matters of finance, as there is in law or any other science. Of course finance is a science, as law is a science, as geometry and mathematics are sciences; but political economy and the social sciences are not real sciences. Of course I may be told that political economy is part mathematics and part law, and that since mathematics and law are sciences, political economy or the social sciences are also sciences. This is most untrue, for the reason that what is called political economy, what is called social science and what is called political science are mostly just a conglomeration of divergent views which have been put together and which cause headaches to the students of such matters when they really have brains from which to suffer. What happens? The doctors of those half-baked sciences try experiments, not in a scientific way and on an infinitely small scale; but all their experiences are nation-wide, and when they are unsuccessful it is a nation-wide failure.
Does the hon. member for Temiseouata believe in Darwin's theory?

I would not offend my hon. friend by telling him that he should not have risen to the occasion. Since the house is in a jovial mood, I remember what was said by a great educator of the city of Quebec, that one should always be able to smile even in his deepest affliction. It is very sad to discuss these matters, but even in war time-the more so during war time-we should come back to fundamentals. Everyone will agree to this. We must come back to fundamentals, and the fundamental of finance is common sense. More than that, it is the responsibility of the government to parliament, and of parliament to the nation. How can we satisfy the legitimate curiosity of our constituents about the expenditures that we vote if we are not in a position to give them all the information that may be asked by any one of them? Even if only one elector, one constituent in only one constituency in Canada, asks for full information about the expenditure of public money by this government, he should be entitled to get the information; and the money spent in gathering and printing it would not be spent in vain; for that citizen is only being true to the old British parliamentary tradition of governmental responsibility in regard to expenditures. I do not want to be cruel to anybody, but I warned the government before my hon. friend the Minister of Finance occupied his present high post. I warned them that a man who was

Interim Supply Bill

responsible for the bankruptcy or failure of a very large United States concern was not qualified to occupy a high post in the Department of Finance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No one in the Department of Finance was responsible for the bankruptcy or failure of a large American concern.
All right; then I ask the minister what his deputy did during the years which are left blank in the parliamentary guide?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What years were they?

Several years. I do not want to be hard on anyone, but I want the minister to have advisers worthy of him. That is all I want; and when that is done I am ready to close my eyes. The years were from 1923 to 1930, when this gentleman was employed by Mr. Hoover in the United States, I do not know whether in connection with the tariff or other matters; it is not stated. But if my information is correct, he was first employed by and later became a director of the S. W. Straus corporation of New York, a very large concern, which among other subsidiaries controlled the Straus Investment corporation, with offices on Fifth avenue. He was treasurer and director of the investment corporation and a director of the parent company. I have asked for this information; the Minister of Finance must remember the time. He was then Minister of National Revenue; and when I brought the matter before either the committee or the house, one of his colleagues prevented me from mentioning these facts. Therefore I could not say anything; I have not said anything then. It is not a question of attacking someone who is not here. It is a question of being free in this country from that sort of intelligentsia which brought revolution in Russia some years ago. I do not want revolution in this country; I want order. And my suggestions regarding the estimates and regarding the public accounts were precisely intended to reestablish order in the finances of this country during the war. It is of the utmost importance that the discussion of public accounts should be orderly. It cannot be orderly unless we have complete figures in the estimates and in the public accounts, so that we may check all expenditures.
That being said, I shall not insist further. I think I have made myself clear enough on the matter. I have no grudge or grouch against anybody, and I have spoken in a very serene manner about matters of the greatest importance to the state as well as to the Canadian people. I shall support the

motion on the understanding that there will be no other motion of the kind and that the estimates and the public accounts are completed according to -the promise that was given to the committee by the Prime Minister last year. There can be no question as to cost, because the presses down at the printing bureau were busy for twenty-four hours a day for weeks, printing propaganda for the plebiscite, and it is my humble view that the printing of detailed information regarding public expenditure is much more important to the people of this country than any futile and frivolous propaganda of that kind.

Mr. Chairman, I have
only a word to add to the suggestions which have been made by the three previous speakers in connection with the organization of debate, and I speak with a great deal of humility as a younger member of this house. I believe most hon. members feel, with the three previous speakers, that some improvement could be made in that respect, and as a younger member I think that if we think an improvement could be made we should do something to bring it about. One or two connected matters I shall mention briefly.
A great deal is said about government by order in council. The house has been told that some 24,000 orders in council have been passed during the war. It is perfectly evident that if any considerable number of these orders in council had been brought before the house they would not have been passed and the work necessary to get on with the war would not have been done. It is obvious therefore that we must have orders in council to do things that must be done quickly. On the other hand this does not dispose of the objection that parliament's powers are gradually being removed from it in this way by legislation of a very substantial character. I suggest that if parliament is to remain anything it is time some new device was worked out by which orders in council having a generally legislative character could be periodically brought before parliament, or some committee of parliament, there to be reviewed.
We have an idea in this house-I had when I came-that our system of parliamentary procedure is modelled on the British system. I read the British Hansard as regularly as I can, and I find that it is practically impossible to reconcile the debates and the procedure in the British house with the debates and the procedure here. They are not similar in any respect. I do not suggest to Canadians that they should adopt every British thing as a model, but if you look at the procedure followed in Britain you will find that it has been brought up to date, much more up to date

Interim Supply Bill
to meet the needs of to-day and the needs of the war than ours is. I do not believe our procedure has been looked at dispassionately and constructively for the past fifteen years; consequently I suggest that for this reason, and a good many others which those who have had more experience in the practice of the house may bring forward, the time has come when a committee of this house should be set up to look into the rules of procedure, not so much from the technical point of view as to see how this parliament can better carry on the nation's business, particularly in connection with the war.

I have listened with a great deal of interest to the hon. gentleman who has just spoken (Mr. Claxton), but I cannot follow his argument as to the necessity of orders in council in regard to non-war matters. I can understand the need of orders in council so far as war measures are concerned, but the expansion in that regard during the last two years has been justified because we are at war, and it has been used as an excuse by the government to remove from parliament the opportunity of looking into many matters which should have been dealt with by parliament and not through the medium of order in council.
When the Prime Minister is asked what statutes of this parliament have been abrogated, amended or suspended by order in council, he is unable to answer because there is no record of them. He says to this parliament that the government does not know what statutes passed by parliament have been amended by order in council.
I am glad to see the attitude that is being displayed in recent weeks by so many members in all parts of this house, an attitude for which we on this side have contended from the very beginning of this parliament; that we must once and for all demand our rights as members of this house. We have a duty to perform. Parliament is being emasculated under the guise of the exigencies of war.
The Minister of Finance makes application to the house for the extension of supply for another two months without giving the house what the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party said was so necessary -an examination of the accounts, of the expenditures being made by the government. We as an opposition do not discharge our responsibility as members before the people of this country simply by saying to the government: We give you carte blanche; we will vote one-sixth of the estimates, and further, we will extend the time for examination of the expenditures until the month of July or the early part of August. When we 44561-1754
come to that period, Mr. Chairman, we shall have been sitting here almost five or six months. We shall be desirous of returning home, for a short time in any event, and in the latter days of the session tens of millions of dollars of expenditure which should be looked into will not be examined by parliament at all. Why cannot the estimates be brought down now?

Mr. Chairman, I should like to congratulate my colleague the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) on the clarity and cogency of his remarks. An opportunity should have been taken long ago to call attention to the illusory nature of the claims of the government with respect to peace-time reductions.
When the estimates were brought down some weeks ago-and not since proceeded with-I made a more or less cursory examination to see if there was any justification for the claim which had been headlined to the country that there had been a reduction in peace-time expenditure. I think I can prove the thesis that that statement is not based on fact, according to the figures revealed by the estimates. It is a matter of surprise to me that with one or two possible exceptions the press did not get the true import of the figures, produced, I assume, by government propaganda, at the time the main estimates were tabled.
As was pointed out by the hon. member for Lake Centre, a summary of the main estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1943, appearing at pages 2 and 3 of the estimates, indicates on its face a reduction of 856.215,457.05. As I have said, this reduction was blazoned in headlines all across the country, and it was suggested that the government was performing miracles in retrenchment. As a matter of fact a clear examination of the position reveals the exact opposite. But that was the impression which went out to

Interim Supply Bill
the country, and hitherto it has not been contradicted or exposed as misleading or ill founded.
In actual fact the main estimates for the fiscal year 1942-43 show a considerable increase as compared with the main estimates for the fiscal year 1941-42. The means by which the apparent reduction has been achieved is to lump together, under the total for the fiscal year 1941-42, the main estimates, the supplementary estimates and the further supplementary estimates for that year. It will be recalled that we had three doses of them. The result is that the comparison is between the total estimates for the fiscal year 1941-42 and the main estimates for this fiscal year 1942-43.
Let me recall the position with regard to these supplementaries. The supplementary estimates and the further supplementary estimates for the fiscal year 1941-42 contained an item of S35,000,000, to which the hon. member for Lake Centre has referred, to provide for wheat acreage reduction payments; and an item of 845,000,000 to provide for compensation to the provinces which agreed to vacate the corporation and income tax fields for the duration of the war. These two together amount to $80,000,000. As the minister indicated yesterday, 822,000,000 of the latter amount has been paid out to the provinces, and I believe nearly all the 835,000,000 has been paid out to the western farmers in respect of wheat acreage reduction bonuses. But in this year's estimates for wheat acreage reduction payments the main estimates provide only $5,225,000, a difference of $29,775,000. I suggest that that is not a true picture, because the government has introduced special legislation to replace the wheat acreage reduction payments, and the final or net result will be in all probability in excess of the 835,000,000 provided for last year. In respect of the new wheat policy to take the place of the policy of last year, they have raised the price but they will not tell us what they are getting, they will not tell us what the loss is, they will not tell us what the gain, if any, is, with respect to their dealings in wheat-although we all know that there is no gain, but rather a huge loss every year. I am not particularly complaining about that at the moment. I am trying to expose the position with respect to the press notices sent out with regard to the estimates tabled here in January.
No item comparable to the $45,000,000 voted for the provinces appears in the main estimates for the fiscal year 1942-43, although it is indicated that provision will be made in the
supplementary estimates; and I refer you in that connection to page 11 of the estimates. Consequently in respect to this one item a reduction of $45,000,000 is apparently shown. But that is a most misleading situation, because it is to be paid, and paid doubly, as we know from the figures that were indicated yesterday-very much more than the $45,000,000 voted last year. I suggest to the minister that the correct comparison should be between the main estimates of the two years: the total main estimates for 1941-42, 8433,000,000 in round figures; the total main estimates for 1942-43, $454,000,000.
What does that mean? It means a substantial increase. To be exact, a comparison between the main estimates of the two fiscal years shows an increase in ordinary operations of government to the tune of 821,752,726.09- a huge increase, and one which I do not think is justified in war time. I put myself in the judgment of the country when I make that statement.
I do not believe hon. members have analysed this situation, and I am glad to have the opportunity now to give my views with regard to it and to expose a hollow piece of sham- if that is a parliamentary expression-on the part of the administration towards the people of Canada in respect to these civilian expenditures.
That may be one reason why they have not brought on a discussion of these estimates. The minister says, give us a chance. They have had four months' chance to bring on these estimates. One of the very first things this parliament did was to take away all the rights of private members. You cannot do anything in this parliament unless the government so direct. They call the tune and we are permitted no rights save and except the withholding of supply. Of all the rights that private members have had, all the rights that opposition members have had with relation to this government the only lever we now have on the government is to withhold supply. When we let that right go, we are finished. That is the only right under a set-up whereby we give government business precedence for the whole session. In ordinary peace time there is a supplementary right, the somewhat attenuated right to bring in private members' resolutions. But how many of them are accepted by governments? Not many. To-day there is not a single opportunity for any hon. member to air even a grievance except on a debate on a money bill. Then how far does he get with it?
I want to impress that position not only on the membership of this house but upon the
Interim Supply Bill

people of Canada. It amounts to the abrogation of our functions. What good will it do to revise the rules if you do not revise the will to carry on public business? I was on the revision of the rules committee fifteen or sixteen years ago. The committee did good work. It might have gone much farther, but nobody wanted to be too revolutionary. The mere setting up of codes of operation is not going to cure the evil. The cure has to come from the administration, in listening to reason in connection with .these civilian estimates, and there is no evidence that the government is doing that.
The minister may take credit to himself for having pruned a lot of the estimates. I have no doubt he did so. I know something of how estimates are made up. They are prepared in the first instance by the departmental officials, and I have never known a departmental official in my life who did not want to increase his jurisdiction and his spending power. That is human nature. I am not blaming officials for that; it is the history of bureaucracy wherever you find it, even in a democracy. I have no doubt that the Minister of Finance prunes them and the treasury board prunes them again. That is always done. Nevertheless, unless there is the greatest firmness on the part of those who have the ultimate responsibility, the estimates will grow and grow and grow. In peace time it is almost inevitable, but it should not obtain for a minute in war time.
The primary responsibility is on the members of the administration who have to deal finally with the question of the quantum of the expenditures on the services. Do you mean to tell me that all the peace-time activities of the public works department are still required in Canada when we are practically at a standstill with regard to the operation of public works? Well, I shall have to be shown before I can believe that that is true.
I indicated a moment ago that the increase in ordinary operations of the government amounts to over $21,000,000, and I put the exact figures, as indicated by the two sets of estimates, upon the record. In addition, a further increase will be indicated and evident when the supplementary estimates are brought down-and make no mistake about it, there will be supplementary estimates; there always are-and probably further supplementary estimates will be brought down.
Whereas last year the amount of compensation to the provinces was $45,000,000, the Minister of Finance, in a press release as long ago as January, and again here yesterday on the floor of this chamber, indicated that we would have to pay about $S5,000,000 to the provinces, plus a guarantee with respect to

gasoline. Fortunately that guarantee did not represent much last year, but I venture to say that for the coming year it will represent a huge sum.
A tremendous sum.

It will be so tremendous that the people will be astonished. It may bring them to a sense of realization of how much money the country spends in gasoline in ordinary times, and perhaps we shall get the people of Canada back to the practice of one of the oldest virtues, and I should say the most unfashionable, the practice of thrift. If we can do that it will be a good thing, because we seem to have forgotten that there is such a virtue as thrift.
The total payments to the provinces for the fiscal year will be, we will say, $85,000,000 as opposed to $45,000,000 voted in the estimates last year. That means an increase in that item of $40,000,000, and that is civilian expenditure. It is important; it is necessary. I admit that, and because there is an increase, additional moneys must be raised.
What item is that?

That is the vote to the provinces under the agreements; $45,000,000 last year as compared with $85,000,000 which will be voted in the supplementary estimates this year, plus the estimated deficit in respect of gasoline. That is civilian activity. True, it arises because of a war-time condition, but I hope the government will not pay that out of the war appropriation bill. We have not yet heard whether they will or not, and before this motion is adopted the minister should make that clear. I shall object if it is paid out of the war appropriation bill.
Then there is the legislation with respect to the wheat growers. That will involve a large expenditure either directly or indirectly on the part of the federal treasury as it did last year. Indeed, we may safely assume that in this respect there will be an increase. I do not know what the amounts will be. I do not suppose any reasonable forecast has been made.
The government does not know.
Probably the government does not know. When it put up the price to 90 cents I doubt if it did know.
The opposition wants more.

That is all right; the farmers are entitled to more. Does the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare (Mr. Pottier) say that they are not?

Why does the hon. member criticize it?

Because I am trying to expose the hollowness of the government's contention that there has been a reduction in the civilian activities of this ' administration, and I am right. I say therefore the comparisons that are made in the main estimates, the government blue book itself to which I have referred, are wholly misleading and present to the people of Canada an entirely false impression of the existing situation. I am surprised at the members of the press, who are usually very alert. I am surprised that the gentlemen of the press gallery have not analysed the situation before this and given the people the real facts. The only journal in Canada I can find which has become seized of the situation is the Globe and Mail, and I will take the liberty of putting on the record of this house an editorial of the Globe and Mail of February 23 last under the caption "Few signs of economy". I read:
The federal government tabled on Friday the estimates of the ordinary non-war civilian expenditures for the fiscal year 1942-43 and they will make rather depressing reading for the Canadian public. For the fiscal year 1941-42 the original civilian estimates were $433,131,000 but they were swollen by later supplementary estimates to a total of $509,566,000. Mr. Ilsley now places the civilian requirements for the coming fiscal year at $454,884,000 and there accordingly appears temporarily on the surface a reduction of some $55,000,000, but the decrease is patently illusory. For the 1941-42 estimates included an item of $45,000,000 designed to compensate the provinces for the revenues which they would lose by withdrawing from the field of income taxation upon individuals and corporations. But this sum was not paid over-
I understand that half of it has been paid, but I do not think it was made clear whether it was paid in this fiscal year or in the past fiscal year. The minister should tell us.
But this sum was not paid over, and so the total civilian expenditures in 1941-42 were cut to about $464,500,000. Now if agreements are consummated with all the provinces about the transfer of taxation rights, this compensatory item of $45,000,000, which was not included in the estimates tabled on Friday, will have to be added later; and even if there were no other supplementary estimates, which is unlikely'-
Quite unlikely, I suggest.
-our civilian expenditures for 1942-43 would thus be raised to roughly $500,000,000-[DOT]
Yes, and a good deal more than $500,000,000, depending entirely on what the deficit is in the guaranteed tax.
-which would mean that they will eventually be at least $35,000,000 greater than the total sum required for 1941-42.
I will not read the rest of it, which is along the same line. I ask the minister this question, and it is the appropriate occasion on which to ask it; Why is it that the government has not grappled with this problem of civilian expenditures and endeavoured to lead the country? I heard my hon. friend over the radio suggest that the people of Canada should tighten their belts. What evidence is there that the government is tightening its belt?
They haven't got a belt.
Braces are more secure.

I find them so myself. The people of Canada are asked, in this figure of speech, to tighten their belts; but I repeat, what evidence is there that the government of Canada is tightening its belt? Go through the purlieus of this house and look at the number of men on the House of Commons payroll. Has there been any cut in the personnel of this house? I ask the minister. There has not been any.
Mr. ILSLEY; Now you are getting somewhere.

I am dealing with a situation which comes right under my own nose. There are as many men on the payroll of this house as there ever were. Go to the senate and you will find there men who are actually doing nothing because the government will not give the senate anything to do. They serve a useful purpose and they have to be there. What are these men in the senate doing during the long recesses? They are not doing anything. The government should use the senate. Those fifteen vacancies should be filled with some of the best brains in the country, who could assist the government to carry on the war effort. There are men in the ranks of the Liberal party, and if there are not, there are men in the ranks of the Conservative party, who could help the war effort of the country, and could do wonderful work in the senate of Canada. But because of past considerations, past commitments which ought never to have been made, this cannot be accomplished. Let me impress upon gentlemen who claim to represent minorities the fact that the senate, which was set up by the wisdom of the founding fathers to be the bulwark of minorities in this country, is being allowed, by the action of the administration, to lapse into desuetude and decay.
One other matter. I was interested when the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) brought to his place in the house and exhibited to us the detailed budget of the United States in connection not only
Interim, Supply Bill

with peace-time activities but also with wartime expenditures on the navy and other armed services. What have we that is comparable to that? We get nothing but a few lump sums, without any statement that the amounts indicated be adhered to; they are simply a guide or chart. We have heard about charts before at the hands of my right hon. friend. A chart is something to be disregarded if it is the will of the administration so to do. This House of Commons ought to insist that when the next war appropriation bill comes down, be it $3,000,000,000 or what not, the government, with all the staff they have available, shall produce to the people of Canada and the membership of this house reasonable details of their expenditures, what their proposals are with regard to military expenditures. I serve notice on the administration now that if I am here I shall demand that that be done, and I ought to receive the support of every private member of this house, irrespective of where he sits. Do you know, any one of you, where your money is going? Do you know, any one of you, how much of your money is being wasted through irresponsible officials or appointees of a government who have no responsibility to parliament? You do not, do you? Not one of you. Do you know how much money an aeroplane costs? You have not an idea in the world how much money you are putting into aeroplanes. All these things are done with the taxpayers' money, voted by this parliament more or less willingly I think perhaps for the most part, and as far as I am concerned most willingly. All the money the government want with which to wage this war successfully will be given by the noble Canadian people, who have always been ahead of this government. They will give it to them with the best of grace. But how much are we told as to what is being done with our money and how much of it is wasted?
Let me give an illustration. Early in the war representations were made to this government that they should build an airport at Pennfield, engineers were sent down. I myself thought it might be a proper place to build an airport. When the engineers came back I understood their report was adverse. I took occasion to send for the director and for the engineer who made the inspection, and they gave rather convincing reasons that owing to atmospheric conditions it was not a proper thing to build an airport at Pennfield. I did not agree with them; I do not agree with them yet. But the project was first proceeded with and then abandoned, and the reason given was its proximity to the bay of Fundy. Last Sunday night on my way here, at the railway junction at MacAdam across the track

from me stood a special train, the cost of which would be thousands of dollars, to move to Rivers, Manitoba, the officers and staff that had been at Pennfield. They do not know why they are going, but I believe there has been some condemnation of the establishment of an airport at Pennfield because of certain climatic conditions. This should be explained to us by the Minister of National Defence for Air.
Now, what happened? Notwithstanding the adverse reports that I learned of through the medium I have mentioned, someone some time decided that an airport should be established at Pennfield. A contractor was brought here from New Brunswick, a good contractor with ample plant. He went home with me on the train one day and he had a smile like the smile on the face of a tiger-after he got a contract at his own price. Millions have been spent on that airport, and now it is to be abandoned.
How many millions?

I do not know. I want to know. I am told it is now to be abandoned; that remains to be seen. At all events the school that was there has been moved out lock, stock and barrel. I saw them going myself. That is the type of thing that the people of Canada do not understand and that they want explained. And they want the truth. I venture to say that twenty-five cents out of every dollar-it certainly was true in the early stages of the war -paid for war expenditures was absolutely wasted. Not a dollar's worth of labour or return was given for a dollar of expenditure. Speed was the only thing. And why was speed necessary? Because this government in the first nine months of the war did absolutely nothing to meet the situation. They were going to have a moderate war. A moderate war I Ask any hon. member from the province of Quebec if they were not promised that Canada's contribution would be a moderate contribution.
Promised by whom?
By the Liberal party at the last election. I can turn up in my files dozens of clippings and reported speeches.
What did the hon. member for Essex tell them in Windsor?

I will say to the minister that this debate will have served a useful purpose if it calls the attention of the country to the present situation, and if he will heed the voice of public opinion. It is not right that he should ask for two months'

interim supply and then in the closing days of the session, in July next, when hon. members who have been here for nearly seven months are anxious to get away, seek to pass these estimates. That is not the way parliamentary business should be done.
I commend these considerations to the Minister of Finance. I hope he will take them in good part. I hope there will be some improvement, and I hope that press notices will not be given out, as they were in January last, that in my view are wholly false.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My colleague the Minister of Mines and Resources is I believe about to make a few remarks, but before he does so I want at once to take exception to the suggestion that there was any sham or any falsity about any press statement issued by myself as Minister of Finance. I remember the press release very well. Pains were taken to make it in no way misleading. There was nothing misleading about it, nor was there anything misleading about the summary of expenditures for the last fiscal year or this fiscal year. The hon. gentleman has not suggested any manner in which the presentation could have been improved. The facts were presented exactly as they were, and any interpretation that has been put upon those figures has been put upon them by the hon. gentleman himself. I shall have something more to say about that later.
Of course the minister has not said my interpretation was wrong.
We have listened to a very interesting speech from the leader of the opposition. I only wish he had put as much profitable advice into it as he did sound and fury.

You would not understand
that.
The hon. member for Waterloo North-
Waterloo South.
Then I congratulate the electors of Waterloo North.
They are not so proud either.
My hon. friend has taken a great deal of exception to this interim supply vote. He says, "Why didn't you have your estimates before the house?" They have been before the house.

They
never have been before the house, except pro forma.

Just a moment. The estimates were tabled immediately after the debate on the address was concluded. My hon. friend knows what the situation has been; it has not been possible to get these estimates by departments before the house except on a few occasions. I should like to give the committee a brief summary of the matters which have been discussed since this session opened at the end of January. I agree with the leader of the opposition that the debate on the address dragged on for a great length of time, and that a large number of the speakers who took part in that debate were from the government side. I would not wish to deny him any satisfaction he may get from that fact. But there were other matters. He has referred to the plebiscite debate, which came on after the debate on the address was disposed of. The plebiscite debate did not take nearly as long as the hon. leader of the opposition would suggest.
But it was unnecessary.
There were other measures. For instance, there was a very important measure having to do with the reestablishment in civilian life of those who enlisted in the army.
That was just a bagatelle and did not take any time.
I sat here patiently and listened without interrupting my hon. friend I should be glad if he would accord me the same courtesy.

Quite
right; I apologize to the minister.
They wanted to take it from the elevators and give it to the farmers.
Perhaps it would be a good idea if the hon. member for Waterloo South would hide in an elevator for a while.

Well, you have done
pretty well out of it.
That was the position taken by the hon. member for Lake Centre. What did he advocate? Parity prices for wheat. And the hon. member for Qu'Appelle: parity prices for wheat.
And no bonuses or waste.
Well, it is generally understood that parity prices for wheat would have required probably another $100,000,000 or $120,000,000 on a normal crop.

Is that a government
admission?
Order.
I would ask the hon. member for Waterloo South for once please to restrain himself for a bit.
I just want to know if that is a government admission, that to give parity prices to the wheat farmers would cost $100,000,000. I think we should have an answer.

I am not taking back what I stated a moment ago, that this was the criticism of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle and the hon. member for Lake Centre. First we were not doing enough; we should be spending more money. We should have parity prices for the farmers. They did not offer any calculation as to what that would cost, but on the basis of the representations made it would cost well over $100,000,000. And when these two hon. members were making impassioned pleas for the expenditure of more public money in wheat payments to western Canada, the leader of the opposition was applauding them most heartily.
Would the hon. gentleman allow a question?
I did not interrupt my hon. friend.
I should just like to ask the hon. gentleman if he thinks the farmers should not receive the same consideration as all other producers of war-time necessities.

Now my hon. friend is shifting his ground a bit. I am not criticizing the payments which were made to the wheat fanners, but I am saying that these great apostles of economy advocated in this house a programme which would have meant the expenditure of additional scores of millions of dollars. In that, may I repeat, the hon. member for Lake Centre was ably seconded by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, and both hon. members were applauded by the leader of the opposition, who chastises us this afternoon for our lack of economy. Where is the consistency in that?
And some of the farmers from the west.

I am getting a little tired of these interruptions. The hon. leader of the opposition and the hon. member for Lake Centre have criticized the volume of the estimates for this year. I find myself concerned about that also. I do not think there is any business coming before parliament more important than the matter of providing money for the public service, and finding the means of raising that money. It touches the whole question of taxation-how taxes shall be levied, how the money shall be secured, and how it shall be spent. I agree with the leader of the opposition and the hon. member for Lake Centre that there is no more important duty resting upon parliament than that responsibility. If we go back to earlier days we find that our parliaments had their origin in controversies over that very question, which is, and I think always will be, as long as we have a proper appreciation of our responsibilities as members of parliament, one of the most important matters with which we have to deal. But it is not very often, when you come to consider the expenditure of money, that you hear the voice of economy raised in this house, and I am sometimes alarmed at the extent to which our expenditures have grown. There are, however, many items which are in the nature of fixed expenditures. The leader of the opposition referred to the fact that in these estimates we were voting something over $450,000,000 for the current year. Of that total, in the Department of Finance alone over $226,000,000 is statutory. I do not think my hon. friends or any other hon. member of the house would suggest that we should repudiate or cut down the interest on our debt. I do not hear anyone suggest either here or anywhere else that we should cut down old age pensions.

Increase them.
