On the contrary the argument is that they should be increased. Take another very important item, the amount expended by the Department of Pensions and National Health. The vote there is for almost S55,000,000. Is there any suggestion that practically all this money is not well spent? Most of it goes in pensions to men who returned from the last war and in looking after men who came back broken in body. Is there any suggestion that these pensions should be cut down? I do not hear it, and I do not think you will find it in the house or anywhere else. In these two items alone we have a total of $280,000,000 out of the expenditures of $454,000,000, leaving approximately $175,000,000 for all the other purposes of government, entirely apart from the war appropriation. It may be that in the expenditure of that $175,000,000 some economies could be introduced.
The leader of the opposition referred to the staff of the House of Commons and the staff of the Senate. Possibly you could reduce those staffs, but even if you cut those staffs in two, the saving effected in comparison with the whole expenditure would be negligible. When I say that I am not quarrelling at all with the principle which the leader of the opposition enunciated.
As to whether we should have one month's supply or two, my colleague the Minister of Finance will deal with that. I do not think the government can be fairly criticized because it has not had the estimates before the house up to the present time. It is true that we have had one very large estimate before the house in the appropriation bill which embraces a total expenditure of over $2,000,000,000. Certainly that has been fully discussed. We have spent from twenty-six to twenty-seven sitting days in discussing the war appropriation measure. And so, Mr. Chairman, I come to this conclusion, that while the speeches made by the leader of the opposition and the member for Lake Centre created an interesting diversion in the committee, I do not think they contributed very much to the business of the house.
They certainly put the government on its toes.

If my hon. friend thinks that, he is entitled to get all the satisfaction he can out of it. We have the budget coming along, we have the amendment to the National Resources Mobilization Act, and the strong probability is that the house will not be through by the end of June-
July.

If the house granted only one month's supply, it would mean that the Minister of Finance would have to come back at the end of June for another month's supply, but if we are granted two months' supply now we think we are reasonably sure of getting through. So that while the Minister of Finance may accept supply for one month or two months, I do think the house would be well advised to grant two months' supply.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am very glad that the leader of the opposition and the hon. member for Lake Centre made the speeches they did this afternoon. I want to congratulate them upon discharging their duty, although I cannot congratulate them upon the manner in which they did it or upon the time they selected for doing it. Sound and valid criticism of expenditure is a wholesome practice in this house, and I am sorry there is not more of it rather than less. From the Social Credit party we get nothing but advice to make greater and greater expenditures on the ground that money is easily obtained by government issue. From the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party we get practically nothing in the way of a suggestion for economy of any kind.

I take exception to that. We have suggested great economies in the cutting out of profit in connection with the war effort, where the greatest economy of all could be made. We want more in the way of social legislation, I grant.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Larger expenditures by the government, but higher taxes.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Higher taxes on the rich.
On the rich, yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a fair summary of the position of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party. I am glad that the Conservative party has at last started, even in this imperfect way, to discharge its historic responsibility, which is to criticize the expenditures of the government. It is true that this debate this afternoon is an old-fashioned one, if I may put it that way. It is the kind of debate to which I have listened many times in this house during the past fifteen or sixteen years.
And in which the minister has himself taken part.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have taken part in some of it myself. The practice usually pursued by the opposition is about as follows. In the first place there is a devastating onslaught on
Interim Supply Bill

the government, on general principles, for its total expenditures, just as was done this afternoon. When further dissent is invited to particulars, they show great adroitness in escaping any such temptation.
Speak for yourself.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This afternoon, for example, I was able to get only one concrete suggestion, and that was that we cut down in some way the number of messengers and others who are on the staff of the House of Commons. I said to myself when he had reached that point: now at last we are getting somewhere. I am grateful for the suggestion and I hope that members of the House of Commons will come forward with concrete suggestions of that kind.
Will the minister accept them when they come?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will accept as many of them as are practicable, I can assure you, Mr. Chairman. I sincerely wish that members of the house on this side and in all the opposition parties would show a little more concern than they do about public expenditure.
Would the minister allow me one question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
Does he think it is part of the function of an opposition in urging retrenchment to single out individual items when we have not the known facts in front of us. I do not think that is our function.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Certainly it is. It is the function of the opposition, and it is what a courageous opposition would do. The easiest thing in the world is to do what certain newspapers have done and what the Conservative opposition has done this afternoon-just to take a lump sum and say: There is really no reduction in that lump sum, and there should have been.
I will tell the committee of an incident that took place a year ago when the estimates were in preparation. One of the great newspapers of this country which is strongly and sincerely in favour of governmental economy was criticizing the government, and fairly, from its point of view, for not having further reduced the main expenditures. I think the main estimates as then introduced were $432,000,000, and it was said that we should be able to reduce that total to at least below $400,000,000. About that time a great interest in this country which was generally supposed to be fairly close to the newspaper in ques-

tion was making representations to the government and to treasury board, and curiously enough, just at the very time these editorials were coming out urging economy-it was before the estimates were tabled-the treasury board had before it no less than five submissions from the interest in question for specific increased expenditures.
May we know what that interest was?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No. I must say that they made a very good case for several of these expenditures, and increases were allowed in two or three cases. But the incident showed me that the easiest thing in the world to do is to say to a government: cut down your total amount of expenditure, and if you are not doing it you are showing a callous disregard for the principles which should be followed in time of war. But the hardest thing in the world to do is to select the specific items for reduction.
I want to thank the hon. member for Lake Centre for one remark he made this afternoon. He said that the country was willing to stand any weight of taxation at all. I am going to remind him of that later, and I am going to remind the members of the opposition of that statement later, assuming that he is reflecting the sentiment of the leaders of the opposition. My experience in this house has been this-
Was there not an "if" attached to it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There was no "if". I can almost pick out the members now who, when we get into our estimates, are going to rise and condemn the government for the smallness of certain items in the estimates. I could remind hon. gentlemen of what they have done in this regard during the past three years. I could start with the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) and tell him what he wanted an increase in, and I could go back to the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) who is a particularly serious offender in that regard. He is always advocating higher expenditures. I could go on to an hon. member from Toronto, who is particularly hard on increases in taxation, and so on. I could go over hon. members of the opposition and-

Would the minister permit a suggestion? I do not take exception to what he has said; I do not know whether it is quite in accordance with the fact or not, but I would tell him this: If he wishes a concrete suggestion to decrease the civil expenditures of this government, and wants to know how I think it can be done, he Can do exactly the

Interim Supply Bill
same as all citizens in Canada are having to do to-day; that is, the heavy taxpaying class who have not the income they formerly had, by reason of the fact that they have had to contribute so much more in taxation. If they are going to pay their taxes, as they must, then they must go over every item, and reduce, whether they think it is possible or not. If the minister will say that the civil expenditures of this government will not be $500,000,000 this year because the money is not there, but that they will be $450,000,000 or $400,000,000, he will find a method of doing it, the same as every other citizen in this country is finding a way.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Just as I expected; I did not get a concrete suggestion.

Perhaps the minister will let me give him one, then. In Votes and Proceedings, No. 69, brought down on May 21, there are certain questions with regard to the position of Mr. Adjutor Savard, with the Royal Canadian Air Force overseas. The minister's answer is that he was director of overseas press relations, Department of National Defence, whatever that means, and he was paid $5,800 per annum plus $10 per diem living allowance. I would suggest that there is a case where the minister could do something.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The leader of the opposition thinks that is a good suggestion? That was paid out of the war appropriation.
It does not matter where it came from. It came from the people of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I know that.
And it was wholly unjustified.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It may be that there are salaries which are too high in the service.
The whole position was unjustified.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will deal with the question
of salaries at the proper time; but I wish to say that the government has been fighting salaries, not only in the government but throughout the country, harder than anybody else has been. We have been criticized by business interests, by parliament, and by persons in the service and out of the service because of the rigidity and the severity-what is sometimes called the cruelty and the unreasonableness of trying to keep the salary ceiling on.
That is in private business.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Just a moment; if I am going to make a speech, then I cannot let everybody rush in when they have a stray thought.

Mine was not a stray thought. With respect to salaries, let us consider these dollar-a-year men. In a number of cases they are marked as not having any salary, but as receiving a living allowance of $20 or $25 a day. Would the minister tell me if those are taxable for income?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Absolutely.

Are
they?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes; they certainly are; there is no doubt about it.
In all circumstances?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

Only a portion of
them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, do not get on to the question of taxation of living allowances. No rule of the treasury board has been more resented than that one. It has been regarded as absolutely unfair and unjust. But it has been stuck to, on the ground that living allowances are in the nature of salaries. That is, actual expenses accounted for are not taxable. But if a person is paid a flat sum of so much a day, it is the same as if he were paid so much a year or so much a month, whether he calls it a living allowance, or whatever he calls it.
The government treats all living allowances on that basis?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I shall have to disregard
what the hon. member has said. I was going to complete my discussion with respect to what has been said by the opposition. I am not saying this with respect to any particular opposition. All oppositions are this way; I have seen it go on and heard it go on for many years. The programme, as I say, is to make a general attack on the expenditures of the government, in toto, and to run away completely from specific expenditures. On the contrary they attack the government, and then demand large expenditures.
Mind your own business.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, the hon. member is losing his temper.

No. We will look after our business, and you mind your own.
Interim, Supply Bill

Mr, ILSLEY:	Mr. Chairman, the hon.
member is losing his temper. That is the first time in the house I have ever seen that come over the hon. member for Danforth.
The opposition this afternoon was discharging its duty, and I am discharging my duty now. I am putting this thing in its proper light. I am putting the whole position in its proper light. It must be remembered that this afternoon the government was accused of issuing false statements, and there was mention of issuing a statement which was wholly misleading. The government was accused of extravagance, and of asking people to do things which it was not prepared to do itself. This was done in a pretty highly efficient manner, I think, by the leader of the opposition and the hon. member for Lake Centre. I am putting the position exactly as I see it. The opposition makes its general attaok, and then it runs away from a specific item or a specific suggestion. It attacks us for not spending more on this service or on that service. There will be a lot of items like that in these estimates.
Let us consider the imposition of taxation, that the hon. member for Lake Centre was so very brave about this afternoon. We shall have opposition from every member in the opposition with regard to some item or another, if we undertake to increase taxation. We had it last year; we had it the year before, and we shall have it this year. Just wait and see.
This discussion all started on a matter of interim supply. This is wholly within the control of the opposition, not of the government. If the opposition says that we can have no interim supply I will announce, to-morrow morning, that there will be no interim supply. If the opposition says that we can have one month's interim supply, then we shall have to take one month's interim supply. That month will soon be over, and in the latter part of the month of June we shall have another one of these pleasurable occasions. The hon. member for Temiscouata said this afternoon that this is the last time for him, and that he is not going to agree to the passing of interim supply again-until he has gone into the way in which we are passing our accounts. Then we can expect a midsummer debate, I presume, which will last some days on the question of whether the government is to be given another sixth or twelfth at the end of June.
In my judgment parliament is more and more on trial, at the bar of public opinion. There is something wrong with this House of Commons. I am not reflecting on the 
house, and I do not know what is the cause. But there is something wrong with it. I have asked myself, "Is this the fault of the government, in any way?" Someone rises in his place this afternoon and says that the government has not brought along its main estimates, and asks why the government has ignored parliament. They ask, "Why did they hold their main estimates up?" We placed our main estimates on the table of the house on January 21. We worked day and night to get our main estimates ready in order to put them before parliament, so that parliament would have something before it-if it could get to those estimates. Since that time we have not taken any time off. We have gone on and on; we have sat on holidays-at least, we sat yesterday, at any rate. We have carried out our business-and we have always had an accumulation of business pressing for the attention of parliament. I do not know of any way in the world to get everything before parliament, unless hon. members curtail their discussions or unless we sit all night, or something of that kind.
A lot has been said this afternoon about changing the rules. I believe it was the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), who said that the rules were obsolete and that we should change them. However, he made no suggestion as to the manner in which they should be changed, and his suggestion that the rules be changed did not meet with the approval of the leader of the opposition. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Claxton) said that we should bring our rules up to date. I do not know what he had in mind, but I want to say this-

May I say to the
Minister of Finance that I did not think this was the proper place to make suggestions. I have suggestions which I could make.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Whatever rules we adopt, we are not going to be able to consider more subjects in this house and get through faster unless there is less discussion on each subject in the house itself. Is it the government's fault that so much discussion goes on, that it takes so many days to get through a particular item? I tried just before the Easter recess to crowd the house a little. I will not do it again. If the government starts to crowd the house, the house crowds the government. That always happens. The moment we indicate to the house that we want to get ahead, we simply precipitate speeches about the right of the House of Commons to discuss matters and to discuss them thoroughly.

Interim Supply Bill
What has been the criticism this afternoon? Not that we have put too much before the House of Commons, but that we legislate by order in council, that we have used this power we have of doing almost everything by order in council to "emasculate the House of Commons", if I may employ the language of the hon. member for Lake Centre. If we were to bring along all the important measures which we transact by order in council there would not be, at the rate we are going, enough months in the year in which to get them through. We bring everything we possibly can to the house. We could have enacted our war risk insurance measure by order in council. We specifically had that power in the War Appropriation Act. It is contained not only in that act; in every war appropriation act since 1914 or 1915 there has been the specific power to bring into force a measure for war risk insurance. But out of respect for the House of Commons, and because the subject matter of war risk insurance is peculiarly a field which the house should occupy, I put the measure before them. Time after time we are confronted with these alternatives: Shall we bring this matter before the House of Commons, or shall we deal with it by order in council; and whenever we can, we bring it before the house. The result is that we have to wait from January 21 to some time in June to get our first estimates before the House of Commons. There is no way that we can avoid this unless we neglect something else. The House of Commons at the present time is discussing, as the leader of the opposition said, the biggest money bill which has ever Deen brought before it. We cannot bring peace-time estimates before the house at the same time as it is discussing the others. I have heard that in one legislature in the world two speeches go on at the same time for the purpose of effecting dispatch of business, but I do not suppose that this is the amendment of the rules which the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has in mind.
So here we are. In what way is the government wrong? What could the government have done?

The minister said that just before the Easter vacation he undertook to crowd the House of Commons. I should like to ask him if he did not get pretty good cooperation from hon. gentlemen on this side of the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I got very good cooperation before Easter, but I felt that I would have been further ahead if I had not tried to push quite as hard as I lid. We are strongly
indisposed to tell the house to stop its talk and get ahead, because we do not think we have quite the right to say that. I am simply remarking that I do not know what the government could have done to get these estimates before the house.
I will tell the minister one thing they could have done. They need not have had the plebiscite, or the long adjournment at Easter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is
opening up a very important question of policy, as to which opinions differ, but it seems to me that when an issue of this sort is being discussed, that is scarcely the kind of argument which should be advanced.
One hon. member, I believe the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, said that possibly it was the fault of the opposition. I think that if there were one opposition instead of three oppositions, it could organize its work much better than can possibly be done at the present time.

Do not suggest an
amalgamation 1

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There will be no danger of that. I quite realize that it is just about impossible for three oppositions to coordinate-
Five.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
-their laudable efforts. II
the Conservative opposition were to select their critics on certain features of the government policy and assign them to their tasks, as the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation does; if they were to do that, and I do not see any evidence that they do-

The hon.
gentleman does not look very far.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: which they could have been placed before the house for discussion without crowding out other government business.
Does the minister suggest there was any way that we could have brought them before the house, when the government took away all private members' rights?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No; I am not suggesting
anything like that. The hon. member for Temiscouata-
He is the "unorganized opposition" on the government side.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Temiscouata asks two questions. The first is, is the government prepared to see that the auditor general changes his report so that all expenditures below $35,000 are reported on fully?

Just the same as they
were a few years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am sorry that I am not
aware of the terms of the rule which now prevails in regard to the production of these reports. The auditor general, it must be remembered, is an officer of parliament, and I assume that he presents his reports to parliament in a manner which he thinks is sufficient. I believe I have heard it said that if all expenditures were detailed in the way they were some years ago, an enormous number of volumes would be necessary for their presentation to parliament.

Does the minister not think that is a proper matter to be referred to the public accounts committee, so that the auditor general might explain the situation to the committee, and parliament might determine whether the reports are satisfactory or not?
Did not the Prime Minister make the promise to which the hon. member for Temiscouata referred? If he did, he must have some responsibility in the premises.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, I did not make the promise myself and was not present when it was made, if it was made, and I cannot answer that. As to whether the question of the form which the auditor general's report should take should be left to the public accounts committee, I do not know whether that is a function of that committee or not. I thought the main function of the public accounts committee was to review and probe expenditures which appear in the auditor general's report.

The auditor general cannot appear before this parliament, and therefore we have no opportunity to inquire as to the form and find out whether it is satisfactory or not. The public accounts committee might do it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It might very well. I have not given any consideration to that.
The other question was, why do we not present detailed estimates of our war expenditures, as they do in the United States of America? The book which was produced today is a very thick book. What it contains, I do not know; whether peace expenditures or war expenditures or both, I do not know. I have not seen it. But when we were presenting our estimates of war expenditures to the House of Commons, we considered that we should be very careful of the possible consequences. These estimates, it must be remembered, give a picture of the military plans of the government. When I introduce the war appropriation bill I put on Hansard a brief summary of the war estimates of the government. If hon. members wish that the amounts and the brief summary should be broken down, consideration is given to the request; and if they can be further broken down without revealing information which should not be given-I mean, from the point of view of the public interest in the real sense -that further information is supplied.

In that connection, we have had a break-down of the amounts for the army, the navy and the air force, but no break-down of other items. Could such a break-down be placed on Hansardf There are several other departments which get a share of the money provided by the war appropriation bill, but we have had no details as to how that money is spent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is a good deal easier to ask for a break-down than it is to define a break-down. Break-downs are asked for, and sometimes the person asking thinks that compliance is entirely inadequate. If an indication were given as to the items that were required I do not see any objection.

Take, for instance, the minister's own department, the Department of Finance. Could the expenditures of that department under the war appropriation bill not be broken down-so much for such and such an item, so much for something else, and so on. No one is asking for information which should not be disclosed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If anyone wants that further break-down, I think a further break-down would be possible.

Ways and Means-Interim Supply
Could that be done with each department? It would greatly simplify questioning in the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If the request were specific,
I do not see why more could not be done, but the request should be specific and it should be made, I was going to say, by the leader of the opposition; otherwise every hon. member would want something different.

I have *given some consideration to that point, and I am impressed with the statement the minister made, that estimates are a summary of the government's war plans. I therefore hesitated to ask for greater detail on the theory that perhaps it would not be in the public interest to do so. I am between two opinions. I do not know enough about the question to come to a conclusion, and I should not be blamed for not pressing the matter, because I have not convinced myself that it is the proper course. But there are certain estimates in connection with which more details ought to be given as a matter of course. I will ask the minister in future to give some consideration to that aspect of the situation and to bring down if possible, if it is not against the public interest, estimates in more detail so that members may have them in advance to study them. We do not get them in sufficient time to study them, nor do we get them with sufficient detail. I do not intend to delay the passage of the one-twelfth estimate. I will ask the minister to accept that. This discussion will do some good, both in the house and in the country, and I will ask him to accept the one-twelfth interim supply to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have no option but to accept it. I cannot do anything else; it is as the opposition says. I do not agree with the leader of the opposition at all. I think we would be further ahead in every way if we had two months supply instead of one, but I have no option but to accept the latter.
With regard to civil expenditure economies, as I said, one cannot take totals and compare them; -one must deal with specific individual items, and believe me, the last minister of finance, who was minister from the beginning of the war, now Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), did an almost incredibly efficient job in reducing the estimates for civilian expenditures. I have tried to carry on along the same line and have asked the public to cut out unnecessary expenditures, and I realize that the government must be prepared to show that it is practising what it preaches. I would not say in thousands, but in hundreds of items, therefore-in connection with
every possible item-a considerable amount of time has been devoted to the preparation of the estimates, more time indeed than members of the house have any conception of. I will change the motion, dividing the figures in two, and will ask that they go through.
Motion as amended agreed to.

speechtext:
The house resumed from Friday, May 22, consideration in committee of Bill No. 66, to amend the Canada Evidence Act-Mr. St. Laurent-Mr. Fournier (Hull) in the chair.
On section 1-Definitions.
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of
Justice): When section 1 was called the other day I stated that there were some amendments that were being suggested to extend the provisions to railway, telegraph and express companies and insurance and trust companies. I was under the impression that my colleague the Minister of Fisheries who was beside me at the time had moved the amendments. The amendments were discussed, but I find on reading Hansard that it does not appear that a formal motion was submitted. I will ask my colleague the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) if he will be good enough to move the amendments.
The amendments were read on the former occasion and noted by hon. members who were present at the time. I have a copy for the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson). They are included in Hansard, although no formal motion was submitted.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO MAKE PHOTOGRAPHS OP BOOK ENTRIES ADMISSIBLE IN EVIDENCE
AMENDMENT TO MAKE PHOTOGRAPHS OP BOOK ENTRIES ADMISSIBLE IN EVIDENCE
speechtext:
I regret that I was not here when this matter was under discussion last week. That is, of course, my fault.
The object of this bill is to alter the common law, or the practice, of eight of the Canadian provinces, and, I assume, the practice of the province of Quebec, with which, of course, I am not familiar, by amending the Canada Evidence Act with respect to these matters which are within the jurisdiction of parliament. Having regard to the fact that the same kind of legislation is to be presented to the legislatures of the provinces, there may be uniformity of practice in all jurisdictions.
The law of evidence is a very technical law. It is one of slow growth, and has grown up over many years. Those who are practising lawyers know that no matter how much theory you may have in your mind with respect to the law of evidence, if you are not an efficient trial lawyer you are not able to put into practice the theory which is comprised within the law of evidence.
One of the fundamental things is what is called the best evidence rule. Of course that is based on reason, that the best evidence in the trial of an issue should be the only evidence that a court shall receive. Because at times there is difficulty-I appreciate that

Canada Evidence Act

Mr. Chairman, I did not have the advantage and the privilege of listening to the debate when this matter was before the house on a previous occasion, and so perhaps I am at a slight disadvantage, but I want to say a word of commendation of the proposed change. The leader of the opposition has said that we should not make changes, particularly in fundamental laws, just for the sake of change, and I agree with him in that statement. At the same time we should not resist change just for the sake of preserving old forms, once it is evident that the old forms are not entirely satisfactory.
I have myself seen progress in the matter of court procedure. In the short span of one life considerable changes have taken place. If we go back in history, we shall observe that our court procedure to-day is very much changed compared with what it was one hundred years ago. There was a time when we refused to hear the parties to a suit. The litigants themselves were debarred from giving evidence because the idea was held that the rascals would lie about the case, having a special interest in it. So cases had to be proven without the assistance of those most interested and most intimately in touch with the matters in hand. There was a time when men were put on trial and not allowed to testify in their own defence. They had to bring somebody else to give evidence for them. We have progressed greatly since that time, and largely by a process of making changes step by step for the mere purpose of convenience. Our present system of rejecting all hearsay evidence and insisting on the best evidence only is perhaps a salutary regulation, but it is the cause also of considerable inconvenience. Men in their private capacity and in their business often act upon secondary evidence and form their opinions, and sometimes very accurately, on hearsay evidence. Perhaps we could leave it to courts to give the right weight to evidence if it is secondary and a greater weight to evidence if it is first hand, and relax to a certain extent the rigid rules of evidence to which our forefathers adhered.
This bill is a matter of convenience. It is true that when you relax the severity of your regulations you may open the way for crooks to deceive you. But in life we do that. We do not run our lives on strict rules; we do the best we can and arrive at pretty sound conclusions.
It seems to me that this bill would be real progress because it will not only allow banks to destroy evidence by keeping photographic impressions of previously existing evidence, but also record evidence which

Canada Evidence Act
inevitably will be destroyed. For instance, when a cheque is returned to the drawer it is probably lost to the bank and lost to the parties to some later cause. It has gone into private hands. But if this bill were passed, as I understand it, a photographic copy of the cheque could be kept, if desired, and be a permanent record in the hands of the bank. This would be a convenience.
My hon. friend who preceded me used the word "experiment". He said he was diffident about making an experiment in a matter of courts. Well, all life is a matter of experiment, and all progress must involve some element of experiment. We cannot positively know how things will work out until they are tried, and the trying is an experiment. I do not think we should be afraid of making experiments because, if they do not work, we can go back to the old scheme. If this rule of evidence is found to be too loose, and is abused-I do not think it will be-it could later on be abolished, and we would have added at least that item of experience to our own knowledge.
So I am in favour of this bill as it stands.

Therefore there is no urgency about the amendment; it could be left and dealt with on another occasion if provincial legislatures do enact legislation in that form. If the amendment is not passed at this time and the provinces do adopt that legislation at some other date, a further amendment to the Canada Evidence Act would be submitted. If the amendment is passed at this time, it will be the first step and may become operative when concurred in by the other legislatures.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION

speechtext:
Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Mines and Resources) moved the second reading of Bill No. 18, to amend the Alberta Natural Resources Acts.
He said: When the bill was introduced several weeks ago I gave a brief explanation of the purpose it seeks to carry out. It was in the latter part of March, as I recall.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: March 25.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext:
The explanatory notes
accompanying the bill give a full explanation of the purpose of the measure. It will be recalled that prior to 1930 the federal government had the administration of the natural resources of the prairie provinces. The provinces were in a unique position in that respect since every other province from the time of its entry into confederation had retained full and complete control of all its public domain. When the resources were transferred in 1930 it was found that a substantial number of leases covering various parts of the public

Alberta Natural Resources
domain were outstanding. Those leases had been issued by the federal authority. What we are concerned with in this bill are those leases that cover gas and oil properties.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Issued
prior to the transfer?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: Yes. I said a moment ago that at the time of the transfer leases for various parts of the public domain in the prairie provinces had been issued by the federal authority. The measure with which we are now dealing relates to the oil and gas leases issued in the province of Alberta.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: Was there a termination date in the leases?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext:
The leases were issued under regulations, the authority for which had been granted by the parliament of Canada. The regulations were passed by order in council and they governed the conditions of the leases. At this time there are approximately 810 leases that had been issued covering gas and oil rights, and of those, 169 are in the Turner valley where substantial quantities of crude oil were discovered. As hon. members know, to-day that field is an important source of supply for crude oil for the prairie provinces.
There was no question of the authority of the federal government to vary the terms of the leases. The terms that we are particularly concerned with in this measure are those relating to royalties. But I repeat, there was no question of the power and the right of the federal authority to vary the terms of the leases as far as royalties were concerned. When the resources were transferred and agreements were made between the prairie provinces and the federal authorities, I believe all the agreements contained a section which is known as section 2 in the particular agreement that we have under consideration to-night. That section will be found in the explanatory notes to the bill and it reads:
The province will carry out in accordance with the terms thereof every contract to purchase or lease any crown lands, mines or minerals and every other arrangement whereby any person has become entitled to any interest therein as against the crown, and further agrees not to effect or alter any term of any such contract to purchase, lease or other arrangement by legislation or otherwise, except either with the consent of all the parties thereto other than Canada or in so far as any legislation may apply generally to all similar agreements relating to lands, mines or minerals in the province or to interests therein, irrespective of who may be the parties thereto.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext:
The government is now seeking to give authority to the province to do that very thing?
44561-X76i

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: It was held by the owners of the leases that this section acted as a prohibition on the provincial authority in varying the terms of the leases that had been issued. I believe the legal advisers of the provincial government in Alberta held a contrary view.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Has it
ever been submitted to the courts?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext:
I shall come to that in a
moment. At any rate there appears to be a difference of opinion among the legal fraternity as to the precise meaning of this particular clause. Does this section 2 of the transfer agreement tie those leases for all time, in the matter of royalties for example, to the terms that were set out in the leases when they were issued? Or does it give to the province of Alberta what every other province in Canada enjoys, that is the power to vary the terms in so far as royalties are concerned?
In 1938 a very important question arose in Alberta in connection with the conservation of gas in the producing oil fields in the Turner valley. There was no doubt of the power of the Alberta legislature to pass regulations respecting the utilization of gas. That is, they could pass regulations requiring, for instance, that wells under gas pressure could permit only so much gas per certain unit of time to escape. But if they did that it was held, whether rightly or wrongly I am not prepared to say, that such regulations under section 2 would have to apply generally over the whole province. The Turner valley has been the main source of production of crude oil, but there are other fields in Alberta, which, while smaller as far as production is concerned, are still important. It was recognized, I think by everyone who knew anything about the subject, that while regulations might apply properly and wisely to the development in the Turner valley, they might not apply so wisely or so properly to the development, say in the Wainwright field. Consequently, rather than adopt the tedious procedure of testing the matter in the courts, the federal government and the government of Alberta entered into an agreement to amend the transfer agreement and give to the province of Alberta the powers it sought to enable it to carry out these conservation measures.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext:
I think
the minister is making a substantial omission of fact, and I should like to ask him a question with his permission. Is it not a fact that after the natural resources were transferred to Alberta, they made a claim against the dominion, arising out of the loss of revenue
Alberta Natural Resources

which they contend they would have sustained by reason of the fixture of the royalties? And is it not a fact that an award was made giving them some $5,000,000? I think Mr. JusticeTweedie was one of the arbitrators, and they got paid for this very thing years ago, by the federal authorities. Now they want it twice.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: No.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: I think I am right about that.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext:
No; the compensation
claimed by Alberta was for the part of the public domain that had been alienated.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: Including the petroleum leases.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: The petroleum leases were only a very minor factor, because there was not any question that the Alberta government, as successor to the federal authority, had the power to collect the royalties specified in the leases.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: Undoubtedly.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext:
But large quantities of timber had been alienated, and there were large acreages of public lands which had been alienated. Coal mines had been alienated, and worked out; and the Alberta government had never derived any benefit whatsoever from those alienations. This had taken place over a long period of years, and it was in compensation for these alienations that the claim was set up.
I recall the matter very well, because I was one of a commission of three royal commissioners who adjudicated between the province of Manitoba and the federal government as to the amount of compensation that should be paid Manitoba because of the alienations which had taken place in prior years.
The purpose of the bill is to give the Alberta legislature the power to vary these royalties. As a matter of fact, over a year ago the federal government was approached by the Alberta government, who asked that the agreement be amended at that time. Veiy strong exception was taken to the procedure by, I believe, practically all of those who held oil and gas leases. As a matter of fact, the gas leases are not so important. The real core of the matter is connected with the oil leases.
This happened toward the end of the session a year ago, and I made the suggestion personally to the minister of lands and mines of Alberta that the Alberta government should

endeavour to reach an understanding with the holders of those oil leases, particularly those in the Turner valley. I might interject here that they are the leases mainly concerned. Of the 810 leases I mentioned earlier-which had been issued, a large proportion are in areas where no oil has been produced. I understand many of the leases could be cancelled for failure to conform to the terms of the lease. However, that is not germane to the measure before us.
The Alberta government undertook to vary the terms of the leases, and a court action was instituted. As the leader of the opposition quite properly stated a little rvhile ago, the courts would be the place in which to settle these differences and difficulties, and in which to get a final judgment as to what section 2 in the transfer agreement really meant. But another matter intervened, one which again is directly traceable to the war. We have heard a great deal in recent days, and will probably hear more in days to come, about shortages of gasoline and oil in this country. It is believed, and with substantial reason, that there are other fields in Alberta in addition to the Turner valley, where oil will very likely be found. As a matter of fact, the federal Department of Mines and Resources is this year directing quite a number of its geological parties to the search for oil structures in Alberta. I believe one party is in Saskatchewan. The situation as it existed meant simply this, that the uncertainty was preventing the development of those fields. Those who had oil leases, and who desired to get capital to develop them, found the capital a bit timid because they did not know what royalties might be assessed against them in the future. They did not know whether the Alberta government had the power, or whether section 2 of the transfer agreement was good law.
As a result of this, through negotiations between a large majority of the active oil interests of Alberta and the government of that province an understanding was reached which, if approved, would give that security to capital which would lead to development, and to the possible relief, to a considerable measure, of the stringency in gasoline and oil we have at the present time. The terms of the agreement are set out.
In the first place, all the wells in Turner valley which were producing or were financed for production prior to 31st May, 1941, remain at a royalty of 10 per cent. That is, they were developed and financed on the expectation that the royalty would remain at 10 per cent. For developments subsequent to

Alberta Natural Resources
that date a scale of royalties has been agreed upon, with a minimum of 5 per cent and a maximum of 15 per cent, or an option to the person developing the well of 12i per cent, this to apply not only to federal government leases but equally to a quite substantial number of leases issued by the provincial government, subsequent to their taking over the administration of the resources. This arrangement is to continue for a period of ten years.
As I said a moment ago, it is felt by the oil producers themselves and by the government of Alberta that this will lead to a much greater development than would be possible if the whole question were still in the clouds of uncertainty I mentioned a moment ago.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: Does the minister say, on his authority as a minister, that the leaseholders have agreed to this?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: No; all leaseholders have not agreed to it, but the majority of leaseholders with .active or potentially active properties have agreed. In addition to that, the oil controller was interested in this matter, and he urges-I do not think that is too strong a word-that the agreement should be amended to permit of conditions which will produce stability and get production.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: I do not think that is a factor, at all.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: Did he prepare a brief on it and, if so, could it be made available?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: No; he discussed the matter with Doctor Camsell, deputy minister of mines and resources. That, I believe, covers the main points in the measure. I have no hesitation in recommending this measure to the house. If it should fail to pass I think we would have a period of uncertainty, and consequently a lack of development. Representations have been made to me by those representing the majority oil interests, and they express themselves as wholly favourable to the passing of this legislation. I have no doubt that if it should pass, as I hope it will, it will be beneficial not only to the province of Alberta but to Canada as a whole.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext:
At this stage, Mr. Speaker, I desire to make some observations on this bill. I think hon. members would be well advised to study all its implications. subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext:

that it is the case.

speechtext: How many of them?

speechtext:
I have forgotten at the

speechtext:
I should like the minister to produce evidence that they have agreed. My information is that the leaseholders are afraid to move for fear of what may happen in the future. I think very few of them are willing to take a public stand for fear of jeopardizing the interests which they have in the province and future interests which they may have there.
This seems a rather strange piece of legislation, having regard to the fact that there was a contractual right vested under the laws of Canada prior to the passing of the legislation transferring the natural resources. If there is any doubt about the meaning and interpretation of section 2 in the agreement to which the minister referred, there is a proper tribunal to which to take the case, and that is the Supreme Court of Canada, on a stated case. If the subject matter has been under discussion for at least a year, as the minister has intimated, there has been ample time to have that done and to have' any anomaly and ambiguity in the section settled by the court.
I have not approached this matter of my own motion, but information has come to me from various quarters, from parties who are interested in preserving the contractual rights of certain of the leaseholders, many of whom spent large sums of money in developing these properties, much of which money was lost. Everybody knows that developing an oil field is a highly speculative enterprise, and a great deal of money that has gone into prospecting and development has been lost.
I would point out to the minister and to the house that some of the leaseholders look to the dominion government to preserve their rights in the situation which existed prior to the transfer of the natural resources.
In passing, let me say to the minister that the arbitration tribunal set up by agreement between the former government of Alberta and the government of Canada submitted the case of the natural resources, including petroleum and natural gas, alienated prior to the transfer, and as a result the province of Alberta received very generous compensation from this government. I think that ought to have settled the question once and for all with respect to the rights of the leaseholders,
Alberta Natural Resources

because the people of Canada, under the authority which this government possesses, and under the arrangement between the two governments, paid to the government of Alberta that which they claimed they had lost. That is a factor that must not be lost sight of.
Just in passing, I should like to point out this as a consideration, not a primary consideration by any means, but in recent years the dominion government or the courts, or both, disallowed, or declared ultra vires, many of the acts passed by the legislature of Alberta which had the effect of interfering with contractual rights of mortgagees and vendors under agreements of sale. That I think is a correct statement of the principle.
The federal government is now, I am sure at the instance of the provincial government, initiating legislation which clearly interferes with the contractual rights of individuals made with the dominion long anterior to the transfer of the natural resources. The federal government is moving, not of its own motion in this matter, but at the instance of the government of Alberta.
It is suggested-and I commend this to the minister-that it is improper for the dominion government to sanction and aid in what is considered a breach of trust and a breach of its own agreement under dominion laws, which would only be possible by a legislative enactment such as we now have before us. That is the only way in which this can be done, and such action cannot be justified. I lay that down as a principle. If that is true with respect to the violation of contractual rights under acts passed by the Alberta legislature in 1941, which have been disallowed, then I say that any reasons which would cause the dominion government to disallow such legislation interfering with contracts to which the federal government was not a party would apply with far greater force to the initiation of legislation affecting adversely contracts to which the federal government is a party. I lay that down as a principle of law for the guidance of the minister. He ought to think about that and give some attention to it.
I am advised-I do not know how correct my advice is-that not one single holder of a dominion licence favours this legislation.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: That is not correct.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: Then I ask the minister to produce evidence of its incorrectness; I think we are entitled to that. I do say this, that not one of these companies can afford to come out into the open and fight this sort of thing because of the fear of the wrath to come later on.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: Particularly if they hold a provincial lease.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: Absolutely, and most of them are under the jurisdiction of the provincial government. It is human nature, just the same as it is human nature to them to look to this parliament to see that they are given fair play. I think this parliament ought to see that they are given fair play.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: We are giving them fair play for a lifetime if we give them royalties for all time.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext:
There is no doubt that the leaseholders spent their money and took a chance. A great number of them sank their money in the venture; some of them won, and many lost. That is true of all such developments. I think the whole effect of this legislation, as far as I have been able to study the case, is that, in effect, it will be a breech of trust with the original leaseholders. That is my view.
I have before me a submission with respect to the history of this transaction. I am going to take a little time to read parts of it and to comment on it.
Prior to the transfer of the natural resources by the dominion to the province of Alberta pursuant to the natural resources agreement of 1929, a large number of agreements between the dominion and individuals and companies were entered into. These dealt, as the minister has very properly said, with dominion lands, but included, among other things, leases of petroleum and natural gas.
Large expenditures were made by companies and individuals, by holders of the leases, in exploring and drilling for oil in Alberta during the period from 1914 down to the date of the agreement.
Many of these leases were issued and were subject to and developed on the strength of regulations approved by order in council of this government under date of March 11, 1911, and these provided, among other things, the following:
No royalty shall be charged upon the sales of the petroleum acquired from the crown under the provisions of the regulations up to the first day of January, 1930, but provision shall be made in the leases issued for such rights that after the above date the petroleum products of the location shall be subject to whatever regulation in respect of the payment of royalty may then or thereafter be made.
That, of course, was an inducement for people who put out their money to make these
researches and to explore and drill for oil.

Alberta Natural Resources
If they struck oil, well and good; if they did not strike oil, they lost on the speculation.
The order in council goes on to say:
A royalty at such rate as may from time to time be specified by order in council may be levied and collected on the natural gas products of the leasehold.
In 1914, drilling in the Turner valley area was extensively engaged in, and I am informed that millions of dollars were spent by leaseholders in endeavouring to secure production under leases subject to these regulations.
Then followed the great war, and there was a period of stagnation in that area. But the majority of dominion leases comprising central and southern portions of Turner valley were held by lessees at great financial sacrifice, with the result that further developments took place during the several years when oil development was renewed, notably in 1926 and in subsequent years.
The regulations to which I have referred as having been passed under the order in council of 1911 were rescinded, and in 1919 further regulations were made by the federal authority, including, among others, the following:
The sales of the products of any location acquired under the provisions of these regulations shall be subject to the payment to the crown of such royalty thereon as may from time to time be fixed by the governor in council, the royalty to be collected in such manner as may be specified by the minister.
That certainly was narrowing down the time in which there could be no royalty, which under the present arrangement would not accrue until 1930.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION

I come from that part of Alberta which is vitally interested in the oil resources of the one and only province of this dominion which has a potential supply of one of the most vitally necessary commodities for carrying on this war. When this agreement was proposed a year ago I offered objection to it, in that I, too, felt that the dominion government should not alter what was considered to be a binding, contractual obligation of this government with those people, firms and corporations, who had taken oil and petroleum leases from this government on terms and conditions which were, at least in their minds, and in that of the investing public, clear and unambiguous, namely, that the royalty was fixed and certain. The order in council was passed in 1920 to make the matter certain and to give a feeling
of security to those adventurers who might be interested in investing their money in exploring the oil potentialities of Alberta and the subsequent development of them. It was because of the very uncertainty which had existed up to that time that men were loath to spend the enormous sums necessary, particularly in southern Alberta, because of the peculiar and difficult rock formation and the depth to which it had been determined drilling had to be carried in order to ensure production. It was not an uncommon thing for an oil well to cost in those days anywhere from 8150,000 to 8300,000.

Yes; some as high as $500,000. No person was going to gamble any such sum unless he knew with some degree of certainty what portion or share of whatever he did find would have to go to the crown. That was the reason why the order in council was passed in 1920, as the recital to the order in council states. It was to give certainty where uncertainty had theretofore existed, and that certainty was given to encourage and ensure the development and the expenditure of the large sums necessary not only to locate but to develop the oil resources of the province. There is not a shadow of doubt that, from that time on, the holders of all leases issued by the federal authority and, up until as late as a year ago, the provincial authority, felt that that regulation or that order in council was binding in so far as any federal leases were concerned which had been issued prior to October, 1930, when the actual transfer of the resources took place and the oil and petroleum resources passed to the provincial government.
At the time the Alberta resources agreement was entered into the government of the dominion deemed it necessary and prudent, and I think wholly justified, to insert clause 2 in that agreement, which provided that the provincial government as such would carry out in accordance with the terms of the existing leases all their covenants and agreements, included in which I believe, and certainly every federal leaseholder believed, was the term or stipulation in regard to royalty, which would go to the provincial government instead oi to the federal government. The oil industry in Alberta has carried on in reliance upon that up to the present time, and even as late as last year denied the right and the jurisdiction of the provincial government to change the royalty stipulations in any of the outstanding federal leases. I thought at the time, and I so intimated, that before the federal government agreed to any alteration in the terms of the Alberta resources agreement, the

Alberta Natural Resources

least it should do was to consult with and get the consent of those leaseholders who had dealt with it in good faith and had invested their money in oil leases on the strength of those orders in council which were in effect at the time they got their leases.
So the bill was not introduced in this house a year ago. But it was ratified by the legislature of Alberta. And the Alberta governs ment, as any one from that province knows, notwithstanding the fact that the agreement had not been ratified by the federal government proceeded to enforce or try to enforce the increased royalties. Not one of the old federal leaseholders paid the 'increased royalty demanded by the provincial government. I understand on very good authority that the provincial government decided to make an issue of it, decided to start a lawsuit against one of the biggest oil operators to enforce payment of the increased royalty. But then they thought better of it, and following the usual custom and practice now of the government of Alberta they decided that instead of going to the courts and trying to enforce their legislation, they had better refer the legislation itself to the courts to find out whether it was valid. That is the procedure that was adopted. The Alberta attorney general is none other than the premier himself; he has no legally trained attorney general. Several years ago he fired the only one he had, and the result is that in the interval this parliament and the courts of this country have disallowed or set aside more Alberta legislation than legislation enacted by any other province since confederation. As late as March 28 of this year this government disallowed three acts passed by the Alberta legislature. They all related for the most part to contractual rights and obligations. They were the debt suspension act of 1941, the orderly payment of land debts act, and the limitation of actions act of 1935 amendment act of 1941. Any one in Alberta knows of the numerous acts of the Alberta legislature relating to debts which have been declared ultra vires by the courts.
Instead of pursuing a lawsuit as I indicated, the Alberta government referred their new royalty legislation to the supreme court of Alberta to ascertain in advance, if possible, whether it was good or bad. Then they thought better of that, and representatives of the government got together with certain of the larger leaseholders and operators and entered into a deal. Those with whom the deal was made are those parties or leaseholders referred to in the schedule to this agreement. In effect, the deal was this: "If you will support this bill and application to the federal government in so far as those federal leases which you have already drilled are concerned we 
will guarantee that you will not pay more than 10 per cent for all time to come. We will go a step further and say that with respect to any provincial leases that you hold, we will agree with you that for the next ten years the maximum royalty that you shall have to pay will be 12i per cent."

As far as I can see, the only thing that is being done is that the dominion government is releasing the rights and protection it gives to these minority leaseholders, and turning them over to the province of Alberta. How in the world can action like that be conducive to producing oil in Alberta, in view of the record of the Alberta government in the past in connection with its contractual obligations?
On that point it seems to me that if the minister wished to have stability, and if this government wished to have stability, as far as the leaseholders are concerned, he should have entered into an agreement with the provincial government which would have provided specifically that those leaseholders who acquired their interest before 1930, and who come within the provision of the legislation referred to, and are described as not having financed or proceeded with their leaseholds, would have been protected, and that the royalties which would be charged to them would not exceed 10 per cent. If that were

done, it would give them stability. The province of Alberta would know where they were, and the Dominion of Canada would have complied with the trust reposed in it on behalf of these minority leaseholders.
I suggest to the minister and to the house that this is a breach of the fiduciary relationship between these minority leaseholders and the dominion government. As pointed out by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson), on March 25 the minister advised the house that he would table the correspondence he had received in this connection. He has not yet done so. Surely there must have been some objection to the passing of this legislation. Surely those persons who were interested in this field, and who were not in the position of being squeezed, if I may use that expression, because of the fact that they own provincial leases, have made some representations to the administration as to the advisability of not proceeding with this legislation. [DOT]
Due to the fact that the minister agreed to table the correspondence, I suggest that he should do so, and that we should have an opportunity of examining it before proceeding further. There are various things which occur to me and which seem rather strange in connection with this matter. In the first place the minister suggested that one of the reasons was the fact that they did not wish to proceed through the courts, and to spend all that length of time which he felt would be entailed in court proceedings. Well, this matter arose a year ago and, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Edwards), the agreement is predated to May 31, 1941. If the federal administration had wanted to obtain the opinion of the court, they could easily have done so in that interval.
In any event, why should they assume the onus of discharging a responsibility which is purely that of the province of Alberta? Why should they assume the onus of the possibility of having actions for damages brought against them by these minority leaseholders? I wonder if the minister has considered that point. I wonder if he has asked for an opinion from the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) and if he has ascertained whether these people would have an action against the dominion government for damages, if this legislation is proceeded with? The minister shakes his head. Has he obtained an opinion from the Minister of Justice on the point?
There is this further very important point. The leader of the opposition referred to the question of constitutionality. I believe there is a duty upon the administration to ascertain from its advisers whether this procedure is

Alberta Natural Resources
constitutionally possible and whether, in view of the fact that the original legislation was sanctioned by an act of this parliament and had to be taken from here to the imperial parliament in Great Britain, an amendment like this would also have to be taken to the imperial parliament. I am not suggesting that it should, nor am I expressing any opinion in the matter. But in view of the fact that that action was taken before, can the minister assure us that it is not necessary in the present instance?
The memorandum of agreement states:
The owners have agreed to withdraw their objections to section 2 being amended as above mentioned provided that the royalty on all wells in the Turner valley field that were producing or financed prior to May 31, 1941, would be fixed for all time at 10 per cent, and that the royalty on all other leases, both dominion and provincial, would be fixed until June 1, 1951, at a graduated rate with a minimum of 5 per cent and a maximum of 15 per cent, the owner having the right to elect to pay 12i per cent.
We are not given very much information there, but the statement is made that "the owners have agreed." Does the government intend us to infer that that refers to the owners in the Turner valley field alone, or that it refers to a majority of the leaseholders who own dominion leaseholds? To whom does it refer? In that connection the minister should inform us how many leaseholds that are not in the Turner valley are affected by this legislation. I know that the other fields are smaller. I have not the personal knowledge of the oil fields of Alberta which hon. members who come from that province have, but there is the Wainwright field and the Vermilion field. Are there any royalties in those fields which were held by dominion leaseholders before 1930, and are they referred to in the statement "the owners have agreed"?
It seems to me that the point raised by the hon. member for Calgary West is particularly cogent that a great many of these leaseholders own provincial and dominion leases together, and consequently a great deal of pressure could be exercised on these individuals because there is no limit to the royalties that may be fixed by the provincial government with respect to provincial leases. These men may have accepted the agreement, but they have accepted it unwillingly. How many have signed the agreement or indicated their willingness to accept it? The people I am mostly concerned about are those who have acquired a right, are getting no quid pro quo and are being absolutely discriminated against by this legislation.
I am not very familiar with the tar sands of northern Alberta, but can the minister assure the house that this legislation will not in any way prejudicially affect the situation there, and will he also state whether, if it does apply, there were dominion leases held there before 1930?
The minister should also explain-he may have done so, but it was not clear to me- what steps were taken to consult the dominion leaseholders. I understand that certain objections were made a year ago by the Alberta association-I am not sure what it is called, but I think it is the Alberta petroleum association-and I should be glad if the minister would give the house the benefit of the objections that were made by the association at that time, and whether the association objected on the ground that the legislation involved a breach of trust. Would the minister also state by what method the dominion government approached the dominion leaseholders with a view to getting their sanction? The minister should give us that information because I do not imagine that the dominion government would proceed unless they had first canvassed the situation carefully.
The minister, during the course of his remarks made a statement which I did not understand, and about which I attempted to question him at the time but was not allowed to do so. Would he explain what he meant by the statement that there was no question about the authority of the dominion government to change the royalties before, and why was it so specifically agreed upon, when the resources were turned over to the provincial government, that no alteration would be made in the agreement except under exceptional circumstances, as set out in the clause referred to by the leader of the opposition a few moments ago?
