I am simply saying that the people spoke in the last election in a voice which is contrary to the voice of the hon. member for Calgary West. In the district of Longview, which is in the heart of the southern Alberta oil fields, his colleague received 104 votes and our candidate received 173. In the district of Royalties, also in the heart of the southern Alberta oil fields, the people gave 71 votes to his colleague and 179 votes to the Social Credit-New Democracy group. The town of Hartell, similarly located, gave 39 votes to a Liberal candidate and 48 to our Social Credit-New Democracy candidate. In every one of those oil field centres the people showed their confidence in the Alberta government by returning Social Credit-New Democracy candidates to this house. I remind my hon. friend of these facts in the hope that he will not so vehemently oppose a government which has been put in office by the will of the people.
As far as the bill is concerned, evidently the minister's conviction is that the passing of it is in the best interests of all-of our war effort at this time when we need oil and gas, and of the country at large. We support the bill.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Starting with the speech delivered by the hon. member for Saskatoon City (Mr. Bence), perhaps I can give him some of the information for which he, quite properly, asked.
He inquired if steps were taken by the federal government to assure itself that the leaseholders were not opposed to this legislation. All I can say in reply to that is that the interests and the gentleman who spoke for them and who made representations to me a year ago against the passing of the legislation at that time were the same gentleman and the same interests who came this year and said that they were in agreement with the Alberta government and desired that the legislation should be passed.
He also raised the question whether a measure of this kind should be passed without reference to the imperial parliament. I think the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Edwards) mentioned the same point. There is a provision in the agreement by which the resources were transferred to Alberta, that reads as follows:
The foregoing provisions of this agreement may be varied by agreement confirmed by concurrent statutes of the parliament of Canada and the legislature of the province.

Alberta Natural Resources
So there does not appear to be any question about the power to amend the agreement in the manner proposed here.
He also raised the question as to the authority to change the royalties, and the hon. member for Calgary West argued, if I understood him aright, that the royalties which existed at the time the resources were transferred to the province of Alberta were the royalties which would govern for all time to come. In that my hon. friend is quite mistaken. I believe the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) also gave currency to that contention.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: That is the interpretation I put upon one of the regulations.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Well, leases which were issued under the authority of the federal government long before any understanding was reached for the transfer of the resources to the western provinces contained a provision to this effect. I shall not read the whole section, because it provides for the period of the lease and how it may be renewable, but it goes on to say:
. . . and also rendering and paying therefor unto His Majesty a royalty at such rate as may from time to time be prescribed by order of the governor general of Canada in council on the products taken out of the said lands, such rent and royalty to be free and clear of and from all rates and taxes and assessments and from all manner of deduction whatsoever except as hereinafter mentioned.
There was another section in the lease, section 16, which touched the conditions of the lease, and let me point out that these leases were all similar in character. This section 16 reads:
And provided further, and it is hereby declared, that this lease is subject in all respects to the regulations of the governor in council relating to petroleum and to any regulations that may be issued in amendment of and in substitution therefor.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: In what year were these passed?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: These were passed away back in 1911, if I remember rightly. At any rate they were the forms of lease under which these leases were given to the people who staked their claims or took whatever steps were necessary to get them. That makes it clear beyond any question of doubt that, if the resources had remained with the federal government, the federal government undoubtedly had power to change the royalties from time to time as it saw fit. It had power to change the terms and many of the conditions under which the leases were issued.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: What about the provisions of the amendment to the regulations passed in 1920, referred to by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson), the preamble to which indicated that because of the uncertainty of the position with respect to royalties they would set these royalties for a certain time after the wells came into production?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: That confirms the point I am making. These leases were issued first in 1910, and in 1911 regulations were passed which were referred to by the leader of the opposition. These regulations did not provide royalties. The royalties were first provided for, I believe, in 1919 and 1920, and the terms under which they were provided were these: For the first five years a maximum of 5 per cent and a minimum of 2^ per cent; for the second five years a minimum of 5 per cent and a maximum of 10 per cent; and thereafter 10 per cent. These were the royalties fixed in the order in council of 1920; but they were not fixed for all time to come at that rate, because under the provisions of the lease I have just read, the federal government had power to vary these royalties. There can be no question of that. It is a very interesting legal point, and I realize that the whole debate is more a debate for lawyers than for laymen. It is, however, an interesting point as to whether or not in clause 2 of the transfer agreement the federal government passed over to the provincial government all the powers that it had exercised and could exercise in respect of these leases. That is the legal point which is in doubt. The leader of the opposition stated in his remarks that that was the question which should be resolved by the courts. As a matter of fact, when the legislation was not proceeded with in the federal parliament a year ago the government of Alberta, as stated by the hon. member for Calgary West, passed a regulation in regard to the leases issued prior to the transfer of the resources by the dominion government assessing such leases at the same rate of royalty as the provincial lease carried. I am not sure what it was, but I think it was 15 per cent. I speak subject to correction on that. That was resisted. Then steps were taken to test this very clause in the courts, and that court action was in progress when the arrangement was reached which this amendment seeks to ratify. Why was that arrangement arrived at?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext:
They could not have been very sure of their legal position.
Alberta Natural Resources

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: It may be that there was doubt in the minds of both parties to the transfer as to their legal position, but I do not pass any opinion on that.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: There was no action. Action was never started. The Alberta government, instead of starting action, made a reference to the supreme court.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: I accept my hon. friend's correction. At any rate it was a reference to test the quality of the law. The situation has changed greatly in the last year. I would draw the attention of hon. members to this fact, that a year ago we were not concerned with an oil shortage, nor were we concerned with the question of rationing. German submarines were not operating on this side of the Atlantic. Tankers carrying oil to Canadian ports had not been sunk, and hon. members are aware of the fact that within the last few months a number have been sunk.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: There is no oil shortage in that area. That is a red herring the minister is now drawing across the trail.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: I should be grateful if my hon. friend would allow me to complete my argument instead of making interjections about red herrings and all that sort of thing.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: There is no oil shortage in Alberta.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: If there is no oil shortage in Alberta, why is rationing in effect in that province?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext:
The
Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) from his place in the house said that Alberta was self-sufficient. Can we depend on what he says? There is no oil shortage in Alberta and consequently no rationing would be needed there.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: Rationing is in effect.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: I know it is in effect, but possibly for another reason.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext:
It is in effect for this reason, that the oil from Alberta can be distributed over a wider territory to serve the needs not only of industry but of agriculture as well. That has changed the whole situation. We do not know what is ahead of us in regard to oil production, and I am passing on to the house only the information that was given me and which I believe is correct. It was given by both sides to the controversy, or to the differences that have existed in the past, and that was as regards the stability which would be secured through the ratification of the amend-

ment to the agreement would be a factor in promoting development. This ratification, may I remind the house, was given in the Alberta legislature practically unanimously, and in that legislature they are not all supporters of the Social Credit government. In fact, there is considerable opposition, I believe, in the Alberta legislature. But according to the information given me it was approved in the Alberta legislature practically unanimously, and I submit that those who had opposed to the Social Credit government there, who come from various parts of the province, would be probably just as jealous, just as desirous and anxious to protect the rights of these leaseholders, as the leader of the opposition or any other member of this house. I think that is a fair statement.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: The point is that the province of Alberta would not give that stability unless they had this legislation.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: That has nothing to do with this.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Except that it is an indication of how these things are valued.
This amendment will give stability for ten years. What is the alternative? Perhaps lengthy actions in the courts, the higher court in Alberta, the Supreme Court of Canada, ultimately the privy council, to decide the question; and that might take two years or more. During that time there is uncertainty, indecision and lack of development. The oil interests recognize that. I admit that there may be something to the argument of the

Alberta Natural Resources
hon. member for Saskatoon and that some holders of dominion leases who are also holders of provincial leases wanted to have some security in the fixation of the royalties on their provincial leases. Well, is that going to hurt development; is that going to hurt anyone? I cannot see it.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: But that might have been given without discriminating against these minority leaseholders.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: There cannot be discrimination against anyone. Wherein does the discrimination lie ?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: In raising the royalties of the old leaseholders illegally.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext:
I submit there is no discrimination. I submit that that very fact will tend to stability and to development, which is something we all want and is greatly needed in this country.
The leader of the opposition argued at considerable length that we were violating a contractual right, or that we were consenting parties to the violation of an understanding that these leaseholders had when they took their leases. I dispute that. We are not violating that, because these leaseholders took their old federal leases on the distinct understanding, explicitly stated in the lease, that the terms of royalty could be varied by the federal government. There is no question of that. As I have said, it is a question whether or not the federal government in section 2 passed that authority over to the provincial government. That is a question which could be settled by the courts, and as a matter of fact that was the question which was sought to be settled by the courts in the reference made in the higher court in Alberta.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: Why was it not left to the courts to determine, rather than coming here?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: One of the chief reasons, as I have stated twice already this evening, is to get a measure of stability which would lead to development, and get production which is badly needed.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: This has been going on for two years, and during that time they could have gone to the courts.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: The question would probably have been fought through the courts. When you find a considerable majority of the active leaseholders in areas where oil is likely to be found, in support of this measure, it is something which should not be thrown lightly aside. I ask the hon. member for Saskatoon City to take my word for that, because I saw the list and I had the representations made to me by the gentlemen who acted on their behalf. When they had agreed to this; when they along with the Alberta government are asking for it; when they got together and settled it in that manner, I think we shall not make any mistake in ratifying that understanding.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext:
They
agreed on the theory that if they did not consent, something worse would happen. That is a species of duress. Individuals are afraid of governments.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: If that were the case, why did they change their attitude from that of the year before? I want my hon. friend to accept my statement that the people who made representations against it a year ago were those who came and made representations in favour of it this year.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext:
I have
given the answer; the answer is that if they did not agree to it, something worse would happen to them.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: I have never had that suggestion made. I do not think there is anything to it.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: I know there is.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Was the agreement not
arrived at as. a result of negotiations which resulted in these leases set out in the schedule to the bill being set at a limit of 10 per cent? Is that not part of the quid pro quo?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext:
No; the reason for that
was, as I stated in my opening remarks, that these leases have been developed and financed on that basis; that was a concession they were able to get

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: It was a concession, though.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Well, I would not say
concession; it was an understanding that was reached. But there is another point. I cannot help feeling that there is in the minds of at least some hon. members a doubt as to the manner in which the Alberta government might deal with these leaseholders. In other words, there is a feeling that the Alberta government perhaps cannot be trusted to do the right thing in the way other governments might be. I am not passing any judgment on the merits or demerits of that point of view. But there is not a province in Canada outside of the prairie provinces that did not have and has not to-day complete control of its resources. For example, if they find oil in New Brunswick the provincial government can assess royalty of 5 per cent or 50 per cent; there is no question about its power, or that of Ontario, British Columbia, Quebec
Alberta Natural Resources

or any other province except the three prairie provinces. The question has yet to be settled as to whether legally the restraints are placed on the provincial governments of the prairie provinces that some people think are implicit in section 2 of the transfer agreement.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext:
What
about the point of compensation under the arbitration?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: Really I do not think the question of compensation applies to oil leases. I believe I am correct in saying that there was no oil discovered in Turner valley when the resources were transferred to Alberta. There was gas in large quantities.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: When was the arbitration?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext:
The arbitration was in
1930.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Oil was discovered in
the Turner valley about 1911 or 1912-that is gasoline, not crude oil; I will correct myself to that extent. Crude oil was discovered much later.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Gasoline does not come
from the ground.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext:
It is only within the last twelve or fifteen years that crude oil has been developed in Alberta. I am pretty sure of that, because I have a recollection of investing some money a number of years ago in the expectation of helping to develop an oil well, and my expectations went for naught.
There was one other point raised by the hon. member for Saskatoon City. There was a question whether any dominion leases were outstanding on the tar sands in northern Alberta. I speak subject to correction, but my definite impression is that no dominion leases are outstanding on those tar sands. Any leases that have been issued were issued subsequent to the transfer of the resources to Alberta.
I do not know that I have much more to say. As I said earlier, I have no hesitation in recommending this legislation to the house.
I do not think any injury is going to be done to any interests. I think the people who are mainly affected desire it. I believe it is in the public interest to stabilize the situation in Alberta by this measure. This should be done in order to get the production of oil which is so badly needed in these days.

Shall the

On section 1-Short title.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Perhaps I should make some observations now that I hoped to make on the motion to go into committee. I suggest to the minister that instead of proceeding with this bill now, he have it referred to one of the standing committees. My reason for asking this is that I should like to hear witnesses and counsel for the different interested parties. I think interested parties should be given a chance to be heard. Pursuant to the agreement under which the natural resources were turned over to the province, a number of lessees feel that they have the right to have their royalties continued at 10 per cent. The province challenges this right. Whether the lessees are correct or whether the province is correct, I shall not discuss here; but assuming that the lessees are correct, there are a number of lessees-I thought there were seven hundred of them-whose contracts will be broken by the province of Alberta if we pass this legislation. Apparently the number of lessees is less than I thought. However few or however many there may be, it is a serious matter for an individual to break his contract. But it is much more serious for a province to break its contract, and it is an extremely serious matter for this parliament to give its consent to a province breaking its contracts.
It has been urged by the minister that it is necessary to pass this bill in order to assist our war effort. If it will assist our war effort, then we should go ahead and break these contracts, but we should compensate the people whose contracts are broken. For my part I should like to be shown how this will help our war effort. I gather from the discussion that it is thought this will stabilize the industry. I wonder if putting a ceiling on these leases would not stabilize the industry just as much as entering into an agreement of this kind to raise royalties would? Let us fix the royalties at what they were a year ago; let us fix them at the 10 per cent which is all these people have had from the time oil was first discovered in Turner valley. If a ceiling were put on, it should stabilize the industry for the duration of the war. That is the proper way to attempt to stabilize the industry. The oil controller can deal only with movable property, with the oil, with the product; he has no control over leases. But this government has control over leases. I wonder if the oil controller considered a fixed ceiling on leases when he expressed the opinion that it

Alberta Natural Resources
would stabilize the oil industry if this legislation were passed. I should like to see this bill go before a committee of this house where we can find out what his opinion really is in so far as this particular phase of the matter is concerned.
One of the companies opposed to this legislation has a great many oil leases that will be affected by the legislation. The name of this company is Okalta Oil company which was organized by W. S. Herron, who was a pioneer in that field. I doubt if there would be a Turner valley oil field to-day if it were not for W. S. Herron. He and Mrs. Herron sacrificed a great deal and suffered many hardships to acquire these leaseholds, develop this oil field and bring it to the point where it is to-day. If we pass this legislation, their holdings will be affected seriously. If it is in the interests of the war effort that we should pass the legislation, then we should compensate these people and others affected for their losses. This compensation should be paid either by the provincial government or by this government. The losses of these people will be in the tens of thousands of dollars; I suppose $100,000 would be a moderate figure at which to fix them, but the uncertainty is so great that one cannot fix them with any definiteness. I submit that the Okalta Oil company and others should have the privilege of appearing before a committee of this house to state their case.
There is another class of case to which I should like to refer. Sixty persons invested $11,200 in 21 per cent royalties in small holdings in the Turner valley field. They are advised by counsel, so I am instructed, that if this legislation passes, this 21 per cent will be wiped out. I shall give some more particulars with regard to it, so that hon. members may see how it will be wiped out. There was a dominion lease granted under which a 10 per cent royalty was reserved. A 2V per cent royalty was then sold to these sixty people for $11,200, paid in cash. The other 871 Per cent was turned over to a company. The property has been developed, and a good producing well now exists on it. The position now is that they are advised by counsel that if this legislation goes through, and that 21 per cent additional royalty is taken by Alberta, the 21 per cent royalty bought and paid for by these sixty people will be lost to them. Who is going to compensate them? It seems to me that they should be compensated. I say it will be lost to them, because their names do not appear in the schedule among those who are being protected.
For these reasons I urge the minister to move that the committee rise, and that the
matter be referred to one of the smaller standing committees of the house which can hear evidence. These sixty people should be represented and should have a chance to be heard before a committee of the house. I submit, too, that the Okalta Oil company should have a chance to be heard.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: In the consideration of a section of the bill I do not think it is in order to move that the committee rise and that the bill be referred to another committee. The house has determined that this bill should be referred to committee of the whole. When the committee of the whole reports, the hon. member might move that the report be not now received, but that the bill be referred to another committee. This is not the stage, however, at which such a motion can be made. It is not permissible for committee of the whole to discharge an order in that way.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext: I wish to make one further point. Certainly I would not want anything I said to have the effect of in any way slowing up the war effort or slowing up the production of oil in the oil fields of Alberta. The point which I endeavoured to make, and which I shall repeat is this, that I thought the same results could be obtained and protection could be given to these minority leaseholders. I felt that the province of Alberta was-and I use the expression advisedly-wielding the big stick, to a certain extent, with respect to provincial leaseholders who held dominion leases, in order to get this legislation through. I felt that if the Alberta government had been willing to give a little more, and protect the dominion leaseholder, with respect to the matters on which we have been speaking, the same results could have been obtained and equity would have been retained for the minority leaseholders.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALITIES ON OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext:
I should like to say a few words on this bill because, as I understand it, both the province of Alberta through its government and the dominion government have reached an agreement which is as satisfactory, I suppose, as any agreement that could have been negotiated between them.
I would draw this to the attention of the committee that this again illustrates the whole situation regarding our natural resources. When the resources are returned to the jurisdiction of the provincial government, that government should have jurisdiction over those resources, and any strings attached to the return ought to be strings that can at least be cut by the province under conditions which the province and the others concerned may agree upon at a later date.
I do not believe in confiscation, but I do believe this, that the natural resources which
Alberta Natural Resources

are the common heritage of the Canadian people are fast being acquired and held in a manner which is against the best interests of this country. I dealt very briefly the other afternoon with oil leases which had been in the hands of a company for a number of years, and about which probably the minister will be able to report on another occasion. We have had so many instances in this dominion of our rich resources being exploited by small groups of people who have acquired them in one way or another and which have not benefited this country as they might have done. We have now a great new resource, a resource which was first of all indicated by the naphtha discovery in 1911 or 1912, and then by the crude oil very much later; I think the minister was right when he said about 1930.
It seems to me that instead of discussing the question of leases and royalties, we ought to be finding out upon what basis we can restore this great resource to the Canadian people, so that in this time of stress and strain and in the post-war period we can utilize this resource for the building up of a better Canada. I dislike very much sitting and hearing discussions in this house and seeing bills which, though they may not be designed to do so, nevertheless have the effect of still keeping away from the Canadian people the right to benefit wholly from the resources which nature has placed in this dominion and under its soil.
I realize, of course, that we live under a system which is based on property rights. I do not believe in taking property rights away without compensation, that compensation to end within a measurable period of time. I realize that we live under such a system and that it is very difficult to get away from it. But I want to lift my voice in this house to say briefly to-night that this alienation of our natural resources to private interests should cease and that we should find ways and means of restoring resources of this kind to the Canadian people in order that they may be used for the benefit of the Canadian people.
Section stands.
Progress reported.
